questionStem: A 1-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of low-grade fever and watery diarrhea . She has had 8 to 10 watery stools daily that contain mucus but no blood ; she has had fewer wet diapers than usual. She has not had vomiting or symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection , but her father reports that she became very fussy earlier today. She has been drinking juice and children's electrolyte supplement but not eating much food . Her older brother had a mild upper respiratory tract infection and diarrhea last week . On arrival , she appears lethargic . She is at the 25th percentile for length and weight. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 160/min , respirations are 30/min , and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. The mucous membranes are dry. The lungs are clear to auscultation . questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of watery diarrhea and vomiting . During this period , he has not had an appetite for food but has been drinking sugar-free soda. There has not been any change in urinary output. On arrival , he is alert and interactive . His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination shows a soft, nontender abdomen and no organomegaly . Bowel sounds are normal. Serum studies show: Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Na• K+ cI ­ HC0 3- Glucose 140 mEq/L 4.5 mEq/L 110 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 45 mg/dl Prolonged vomiting with inability to maintain adequate oral intake and diarrhea can lead to clinically significant levels of dehydration and starvation ketosis. In this case, the child has adequate fluid intake and does not demonstrate signs of dehydration but has had inadequate caloric intake. Starvation ketosis occurs when glycogen stores in the liver have been exhausted, typically after one day of fasting. Following this, blood glucose is maintained primarily through the breakdown of muscle and fat to provide substrates for hepatic gluconeogenesis. After approximately 3 days of fasting, adipose cells and their stored fatty acids become the primary source for energy through the production of ketone bodies. This patient's laboratory values, including profound hypoglycemia, decreased bicarbonate, and increased anion gap are suggestive of starvation ketoacidosis in acute illness, prolonged fasting from persistent vomiting and diarrhea, and inadequate caloric intake. Starvation ketoacidosis is a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. If serum or urine ketones were measured, they would be increased. Production of ketone bodies will continue to provide the brain with an energy source during prolonged fasting.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adrenal insufficiency {Choice A) may occur in a patient taking chronic glucocorticoids who becomes ill and does not receive any additional glucocorticoid to compensate for the state of acute illness. Insufficient adrenal production of glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids would cause hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypernatremia, none of which are present in this patient. Fatty acid oxidation defect {Choice B) would prevent formation of ketones. Instead, this patient is successfully producing ketones in response to a starvation state caused by an acute illness. His alert and interactive state supports that he is generating enough fuel for his brain in the form of ketones and thus must have functional fatty acid oxidation. Fructose 1-phosphate aldolase deficiency {Choice C) causes hereditary fructose intolerance. This typically presents when fructose-containing foods such as fruit and fruit juice is introduced into the diet. Affected children develop hypoglycemia and vomiting after fructose ingestion. This child's illness is acute and he has not been ingesting fructose. Insulin deficiency {Choice E) is the cause of diabetic ketoacidosis (OKA). Like starvation ketosis, OKA shows decreased bicarbonate, increased anion gap, and presence of ketones. However, unlike starvation ketosis which demonstrates hypoglycemia, OKA is associated with hyperglycemia. Educational Objective: Decreased caloric intake secondary to prolonged vomiting and diarrhea can lead to hypoglycemia and starvation ketosis. This can cause a metabolic acidosis characterized by decreased bicarbonate and an increased anion gap. Serum and urine ketones will be increased.

questionStem: A 10-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department because of poor feeding and drowsiness for the past day. He also has had two episodes of vomiting today. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and weighed 3600 g (7 lb 15 oz). On arrival , he is lethargic . His skin color is a shade darker than his parents' skin color. His temperature is 36.1 °C (97°F), pulse is 180/min, respirations are 70/min , and blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. The anterior fontanel is sunken , and the scalp has sparse fine blond hairs. The nipples and scrotum are darkly pigmented. The pupils are equal , round , and reactive to light and accommodation . There is no scleral icterus . The lungs are clear to auscultation . Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm and no murmurs . S 1 and S2 are normal. The abdomen is soft with no masses or organomegaly . Genital development is Tanner stage 1; the penis is 4 cm long. Testes are descended . Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following?
correctExplanation: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis, particularly of cortisol, with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. Because of decreased production of hormones, the adrenal gland is stimulated by the pituitary in an attempt to increase hormone production, leading to adrenal hyperplasia, the namesake of this condition. The most common form of CAH and the cause of this patient's manifestations is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents with salt wasting in a newborn or precocious puberty in a child, as well as virilization of infants with an XX karyotype (eg, clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion), caused by increased concentrations of androgens. Because of the enzyme deficiency, concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and testosterone are increased, while aldosterone and cortisol are decreased, leading to hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia (caused by inadequate cortisol). Diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin, as seen in this newborn, is characteristic. Melanin production is regulated in part by melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH). MSH is a byproduct of proopiomelanocortin (POMC) which also produces adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In adrenal insufficiency, stimulation of ACTH production by POMC simultaneously produces MSH, leading to diffuse hyperpigmentation in affected patients. Treatment of CAH consists of exogenous glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid supplementation.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. When present, aldosterone binds to receptors in the collecting tubule of the nephron and leads to placement of sodium and potassium channels on the luminal cell membrane. Potassium exits the cell through the channel and into the lumen. Without aldosterone, potassium does not leave the cell and instead accumulates in the interstitium and blood, causing increased serum potassium, not decreased serum potassium (Choices A, C, and E). Without elimination of potassium, there is no gradient by which sodium reenters the cell. Instead, sodium remains in the lumen and is lost in the urine. This is called salt wasting and is accompanied by a decreased serum sodium, not normal (Choice F) or increased sodium (Choice D). Educational Objective: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia results from a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis. Its most common form, 21-hydroxylase deficiency, presents with salt wasting in infants or precocious puberty in children. It also causes the virilization of XX infants, increased concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Treatment includes the exogenous administration of mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids.

questionStem: A 2½-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because she is concerned about his language development. He uses fewer words than his two older siblings did at the same age. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . He began walking at the age of 11 months. He feeds himself , plays well with his siblings , and does well in day care. Motor development is appropriate for age. He knows 100 words but does not use them in phrases . Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this child's language development?

choices.E: No further evaluation is indicated at this time

correctExplanation: Children with developmental delay should undergo audiometry to evaluate for hearing loss. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. Hearing loss in children may occur because of either conductive or sensorineural etiologies. A careful history and general physical examination should be performed to evaluate for possible syndromic features. Weber and Rinne tests can distinguish conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine audiometry screening for all school-aged children.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intelligence testing (Choice A) is not an appropriate initial test for isolated delay in language development. This child's isolated delay in language development with otherwise normal developmental milestones is more concerning for hearing loss. Speech evaluation (Choice B) may be useful for identifying abnormalities of speech production. This child has a low-normal vocabulary for his age. While speech evaluation may be warranted, audiometry should be performed first. MRI of the inner ears (Choice D) may be indicated based on the results of audiometry and a careful physical examination but is not an appropriate initial test. No further evaluation is indicated at this time (Choice E) is incorrect. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. Educational Objective: Children with developmental delay should undergo audiometry to evaluate for hearing loss. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine audiometry screening for all school-aged children.

questionStem: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the physician 4 days after her sexual partner was diagnosed with gonorrhea . Examination shows no abnormalities . Tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are ordered . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Oral azithromycin and intramuscular penicillin therapy
choices.E: No treatment indicated because the patient is asymptomatic

correctExplanation: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative diplococcus and can cause vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Vaginitis typically presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus. Cervicitis presents with similar discharge, but also with an erythematous, friable cervix and cervical motion tenderness on examination. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, PID with purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms such as fever can result. If left untreated, PID can become complicated by a tuba-ovarian abscess or intraabdominal abscess, presenting with focal tenderness and a fluctuant mass; it can cause consequent infertility. Gonorrhea can present with dissemination (tenosynovitis, dermatitis, polyarthralgia) or reactive arthritis. Risk factors for the development of gonorrhea include multiple sexual partners, new sexual partners, receptive anal intercourse, a young age, substance abuse, and inconsistent condom usage. Coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis is common, therefore treatment typically consists of ceftriaxone and doxycycline, with the latter covering a possible concurrent chlamydia! infection while confirmatory tests are pending. In a high-risk exposure to gonorrhea, empiric treatment to cover both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis is appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intramuscular ceftriaxone therapy only (Choice A) would treat gonorrhea. However, risk for coinfection with C. trachomatis is high, and this antibiotic regimen would not cover a chlamydia! infection. Oral azithromycin therapy only (Choice C) would treat a chlamydia! infection. However, this patient has been exposed to gonorrhea and requires additional treatment with ceftriaxone. Oral azithromycin and intramuscular penicillin therapy (Choice D) would cover a chlamydia! infection but would not cover gonorrhea, as N. gonorrhoeae has become increasingly resistant to penicillin. Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline would provide better coverage. No treatment indicated because the patient is asymptomatic (Choice E) is inappropriate, as failure to diagnose and treat this patient could lead to a multitude of complications, such as reactive arthritis, disseminated gonococcal infection, and pelvic inflammatory disease with consequent infertility. She has had a high-risk exposure to gonorrhea and empiric treatment is more appropriate. Educational Objective: N. gonorrhoeae can present with vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Following a high-risk exposure, empiric treatment with ceftriaxone and doxycycline, with the latter covering a possible concurrent C. trachomatis infection, is appropriate while confirmatory tests are pending.

questionStem: A previously healthy 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of moderate groin pain since he participated in a hockey game 24 hours ago. He recalls no trauma or injury to this area. He reports a decreased appetite today. He has not had fever. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows edema of the left aspect of the scrotum . There is marked tenderness to palpation of the superior aspect of the left testicle ; the pain does not improve with elevation of the testicle . A 3-mm area of bluish discoloration overlays the point of maximal tenderness ; there is no erythema . Cremasteric reflex is intact. Genital and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac, resulting in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow to the testis. Patients typically present with acute, severe testicular pain with diffuse tenderness and swelling and an absent cremasteric reflex. In contrast, patients with torsion of the appendix testis present with groin pain, a nontender testicle, a tender, palpable localized mass adjacent to one pole of the testicle, and an intact cremasteric reflex. The appendix testis is a vestigial structure, typically on the anterior and superior aspect of the testis and has a pedunculated shape that may predispose it to torsion. When torsed, the appendix testis may appear as a small blue or black mass in the scrotum. The diagnosis may be made clinically, or with ultrasound in cases where testicular torsion cannot be excluded. While patients with testicular torsion require surgical detorsion and orchiopexy to prevent infertility, management of torsion of the appendix testis is generally supportive, with analgesics and scrotal support.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Epididymitis (Choice A) is a common cause of painful scrotal swelling and refers to acute infection and inflammation of the epididymis. In younger males, this is commonly secondary to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Patients with epididymitis may have moderate pain relief with elevation of the testis. Incarcerated hernia (Choice B) refers to the contents of a hernia becoming trapped in the hernia defect, unable to be reduced to native position. If this type of hernia contains bowel, an obstruction can result. An inguinal hernia can become incarcerated, but this would typically present with severe tenderness and a larger mass with swelling in the inguinal area. Orchitis (Choice C) is inflammation of the testes that results from an infection, sometimes from the paramyxovirus that causes mumps. Clinical manifestations include fever, myalgias, and fatigue. Especially when it occurs after puberty, it is a risk factor for infertility. Testicular hematoma (Choice D) can occur in blunt scrotal trauma and presents with testicular swelling, warmth, and pain. A 3-mm area of bluish discoloration is more likely caused by torsion of an appendix testis, not testicular hematoma, especially with no history of trauma. Educational Objective: The appendix testis is a vestigial structure, typically on the anterior and superior aspect of the testis and has a pedunculated shape that may predispose it to torsion. Patients with torsion of the appendix testis present with groin pain, a nontender testicle, a tender palpable localized mass adjacent to the testicle, and an intact cremasteric reflex.

questionStem: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination . He completed a 1-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by a 5-day course of amoxicillin for pneumococcal pneumonia 2 weeks ago and has been asymptomatic since then. He has had six episodes of acute otitis media during the past 6 months. Immunizations are up-to-date . He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Tympanic membranes are dull with clear effusions. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Lymphocytes Monocytes Platelet count Serum lgA lgE lgG lgM Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment of this patient's underlying condition?
correctExplanation: 12 g/dL 8500/mm 3 40% 50% 10% 420,000/mm 3 10 mg/dL 10 IU/mL 100 mg/dL 20 mg/dL Monthly infusions of immune globulin should be given to this patient with a likely diagnosis of X-linked agammaglobulinemia. X-linked agammaglobulinemia is defined by defects in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which is necessary for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. Deficiency of this enzyme results in failed B lymphocyte development. As B lymphocytes are responsible for secreting immunoglobulins once they differentiate into plasma cells, a defect in B lymphocyte maturation leads to a dearth of plasma cells and severely decreased immunoglobulin concentrations of every class, including lgM, lgG, lgE, and lgA. Patients present with recurrent infections caused by impaired humoral immunity, and treatment is with intravenous immunoglobulin concentrates.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Amoxicillin prophylaxis (Choice A) is given to patients with congenital heart disease or those with a history of endocarditis who are undergoing certain procedures. While amoxicillin would likely treat his recurrent episodes of otitis media, it would not correct the underlying problem. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy (Choice B) is used to stimulate production of granulocytes in patients receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy; it is not the treatment for agammaglobulinemia. Oral prednisone therapy (Choice C) results in immunosuppression and an increased risk for infections. This would not be an appropriate therapeutic option for this patient. Splenectomy (Choice E) is employed occasionally for patients with refractory hereditary spherocytosis who develop debilitating anemia. Splenectomy generally increases the risk for infection with encapsulated organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Educational Objective: Patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia have mutations in the BTK gene, which encodes a tyrosine kinase essential for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. They present with recurrent infections and decreased or absent concentrations of all immunoglobulin subclasses. Treatment is with intravenous immune globulin.

questionStem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was found in his grandmother's bedroom , surrounded by multiple open medication bottles . His grandmother states that her medications include imipramine , phenobarbital , iron supplements , aspirin , and oxycodone . On arrival , the patient is somnolent. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 70/min , respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. The pupils are 2 mm and nonreactive to light. The lungs are clear to auscultation . He is unresponsive to painful stimuli. Ingestion of which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient is intoxicated with oxycodone, an opioid medication. Opioids are central nervous system (CNS) depressants used as analgesics and recreational drugs. Opioids act throughout the CNS and peripheral nervous system and lead to euphoria (caused by interaction with dopamine), altered mental status, sedation, bradycardia (70/min is bradycardia in a 2-year-old patient), hypotension, depressed respiratory drive, and constricted pupils. Specifically, the µ 2 opioid receptor, located in the brainstem respiratory centers and on peripheral chemo- and baroreceptors, controls respiratory depression, which may be severe. Miosis is a distinctive finding that is less common in intoxication with other CNS depressants; it is caused by direct opioid receptor activity in the brain areas responsible for pupillary control. Opioids also act on receptors within the enteric nervous system, reducing gut motility and causing constipation. The treatment of opioid toxicity includes supportive care (eg, respiratory support) and naloxone, a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Aspirin overdose (Choice A) presents with respiratory alkalosis from salicylate stimulus of the medullary respiratory centers, along with high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Tinnitus may also be present. Though depressed mental status may be seen, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and pupillary constriction are more consistent with opioid intoxication. lmipramine overdose (Choice B) typically leads to cardiovascular toxicity (eg, QTc and QRS prolongation), CNS toxicity (eg, sedation, coma, seizures), and anticholinergic toxicity (eg, pupillary dilation, dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention). Pupillary constriction and bradycardia would be atypical. Iron toxicity (Choice C) may lead to free radical production and consequent gastrointestinal distress (eg, pain, nausea, diarrhea, and ultimately bowel obstruction), shock and metabolic acidosis, and hepatotoxicity. Pupillary constriction and bradycardia would be atypical. Phenobarbital (Choice E) is a barbiturate, a CNS depressant that has similar effects in toxicity to alcohol and benzodiazepines. The risk for dangerous respiratory depression is higher in barbiturates than benzodiazepines or alcohol. Pupils are typically a normal size. Educational Objective: Opioid intoxication causes symptoms of CNS depression including sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and hypotension. Miosis differentiates opioid intoxication from many other toxidromes.

questionStem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of a 36-hour history of fever and a 1-day history of pain and swelling of her joints . The pain and swelling began in her right knee, then increased to involve both knees, and has now migrated to her left ankle and left elbow. She is currently unable to walk because of the pain. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat that resolved after 2 days without treatment. She has no known drug allergies . She appears uncomfortable when she moves . She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 136/min, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no rash. There is a grade 2/6, pansystolic , high-pitched murmur that is heard best at the apex and accentuated when she makes a fist. There is mild swelling of the left elbow and both knees; the left elbow and left knee are warm . Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 110 mm/h. An antistreptolysin O titer is 800 Todd/U (N<240) . Salicylate therapy is begun and results in marked improvement of the patient's symptoms . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent a recurrence of this patient's disorder?
correctExplanation: This girl presents with rheumatic fever, characterized by arthritis and mitral regurgitation, following an episode streptococcal pharyngitis. Rheumatic fever is a sequela of untreated group A Streptococcus infection, commonly pharyngitis, in which there is a type II hypersensitivity reaction to self-antigens having a similar structure to, and thus molecularly mimicking streptococcal M protein. Diagnosis is made by the Jones criteria, which describe many of the core clinical features of rheumatic fever. The major criteria include polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea; the minor criteria include fever, leukocytosis, arthralgia, and PR interval prolongation. Patients often have an increased antistreptolysin O titer. Biopsy of affected cardiac tissue discloses a granulomatous reaction with presence of Aschoff bodies. Complications of rheumatic fever include mitral valve inflammation leading to long-term sequelae of chronic mitral valve regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis. Treatment of the initial streptococcal infection is effective for reducing the risk for developing rheumatic fever. Per American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines, once rheumatic fever has developed, treatment includes salicylates and a prolonged course of monthly penicillin treatments to reduce the risk for recurrence and further valvular damage.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Clindamycin (Choice A) and erythromycin (Choice B) are appropriate agents for the primary prevention of rheumatic fever in patients with penicillin allergies but are not most appropriate for secondary prevention of rheumatic fever recurrence in patients without penicillin allergies. Prednisone (Choice D), a corticosteroid, may be useful for reducing inflammation in rheumatic fever, but it does not help prevent disease recurrence. Salicylates reduce inflammation and pain associated with rheumatic fever. No pharmacotherapy is indicated (Choice E) is incorrect. Failure to treat with penicillin increases the patient's risk for recurrences of rheumatic fever with associated mitral valve damage. Educational Objective: Rheumatic fever is a sequela of untreated group A Streptococcus infection, commonly pharyngitis, in which there is a type II hypersensitivity reaction affecting the heart. Severe cardiac damage, including mitral valve regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis may occur, especially if the rheumatic fever is untreated or recurrent. Penicillin is useful for preventing the development and recurrence of rheumatic fever.

questionStem: A 3977-g (8-lb 12-oz) male newborn is delivered at term to a 30-year-old primigravid woman . Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . The mother's hepatitis B status is unknown because she received no prenatal care. Maternal hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) assay is ordered . Examination of the newborn shows no abnormalities . In addition to administration of hepatitis B vaccine (HBV) now, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen for the newborn?

choices.B: Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) only now
choices.C: HBIG at 2 and 6 months of age
choices.D: HBV at 2 and 6 months of age
choices.E: HBIG only if maternal HBsAg is positive and HBV at 2 and 6 months of age

correctExplanation: The recommended schedule of hepatitis B immunization and immunoprophylaxis in newborns is dependent on the maternal HBsAg status. HBsAg assay is an important component of prenatal care and is typically checked at the first prenatal visit. If HBsAg is positive or if there are signs of active maternal hepatitis B infection, the newborn should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine (HBV) intramuscularly and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) as early as possible, with additional doses of HBV at 2 and 6 months of age. In a HBsAg negative mother, only HBV is needed and doses are given at birth, 2 months, and 6 months. As in this case, if the mother's HBsAg status is unknown but there is no evidence of active infection, the newborn should receive HBV within 12 hours and HBIG can be delayed until the maternal serologies have returned. If the serology returns positive for HBsAg, the infant should receive HBIG within 1 week. If the serology returns negative for HBsAg, the newborn does not require HBIG. In either case, the newborn will still require the second and third doses of HBV at 2 and 6 months, respectively.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Observation only (Choice A) without follow-up of the maternal HBsAg titer is not appropriate. If the titer returns positive or unknown, HBIG should be given. HBIG only now (Choice B) is not necessary. Administration of HBIG to a neonate born to a hepatitis B infected mother may occur within the first week of life, which provides adequate time for the maternal HBsAg assay to return. Even if the maternal HBsAg assay is positive, HBIG at 2 and 6 months of age (Choice C) is not necessary. HBV should be given at these time points but HBIG is only needed at birth. HBV at 2 and 6 months of age (Choice D) will be inadequate if the maternal HBsAg titer is positive. Educational Objective: In a mother without prenatal care and an unknown HBsAg status, the newborn should be given the first dose of HBV. HBIG should be given if the maternal HBsAg assay returns positive or remains unknown, but not if it returns negative. In either case, the newborn should receive the full HBV series, which includes additional doses at ages 2 and 6 months.

questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of increased thirst and urination and a 2-day history of decreased activity. Although she had been previously toilet trained and dry at night, she has had several episodes of nocturnal wetting over the past week. She has not had fever, vomiting , or diarrhea. Two weeks ago, she fell off her tricycle , but no injuries were apparent. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Examination shows sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Serum Na + Cl· K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Glucose Creatinine Urine pH Specific gravity Blood Glucose Protein Osmolality 159 mEq/L 125 mEq/L 4.5 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 43 mg/dl 122 mg/dl 1.0 mg/dl 6 1.001 negative negative negative 125 mOsmol/kg Central diabetes insipidus may result from head trauma and is characterized by the inadequate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also known as vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. ADH binds V 2 receptors of the late distal convoluted tubule and the collecting tubule principal cells, which results in the insertion of aquaporin channels in the luminal surface. This results in increased free water absorption and maintains tight regulation of serum osmolality. Inadequate production of ADH by the posterior pituitary gland may occur in various pathologies, such as pituitary tumors, trauma, tuberculosis, or intracranial surgery. This results in a decreased concentration of aquaporin channels inserted within the principal cells of the collecting tubule, leading to an inability to absorb adequate amounts of free water, which causes dilute urine, decreased urine osmolality, hypernatremia, and increased serum osmolality. The hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect this increased serum osmolality, which causes the patient to report extreme thirst. Patients typically also present with production of large volumes of dilute urine, dehydration, and altered mental status. Treatment is with desmopressin, an analog of vasopressin, which results in recovery of free water via aquaporin insertion in the collecting tubule.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Chronic renal failure (Choice A) can have variable etiology, and in children it may be caused by intrinsic renal disease such as polycystic kidney disease, chronic nephritic or nephrotic glomerular disease, or congenital urinary tract abnormalities leading to postrenal obstructive disease. It would be unlikely in this patient with normal creatinine and no history of kidney impairment.

questionStem: A 1-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of increasing irritability and difficulty breathing over the past 6 hours. She has a 3-day history of nasal congestion , cough , and rectal temperatures to 37.5°C (99.5°F). Over the past 2 days, she has been given an over-the-counter cough and cold preparation every 4 hours without improvement , and her parents have been suctioning her nose after applying saline nose drops . She has only breast-fed once in the past 6 hours. Her rectal temperature is 37.3°C (99.1 °F), pulse is 260/min , respirations are 65/min , and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation . The liver edge is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin , and the spleen is not palpable . An ECG is shown . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to an abnormally rapid heart rate and rhythm originating from above the ventricles, typically with a regular rhythm and a narrow QRS complex on ECG. Patients with SVT can manifest with acute symptoms of lightheadedness, palpitations, diaphoresis, and syncope. In infants, signs and symptoms can include pallor, irritability, poor feeding, and cyanosis. Infants who present with SVT typically have a pulse between 220 and 280/min. SVT may be caused by structural defects in the His-Purkinje system (eg, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), or it may be provoked by alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, or psychological stress. In this patient, it may have been provoked by infection or use of an over-the-counter cough and cold preparation, which can contain pseudoephedrine, a sympathomimetic drug that can be used as a nasal decongestant. Because of its sympathomimetic effects, it can cause adverse reactions of tachycardia, anxiety, and palpitations. In patients who are hemodynamically unstable, cardioversion is indicated in the management of SVT. For patients who are hemodynamically stable, attempts can be made to terminate the tachyarrhythmia by vagal maneuvers (eg, ice or cold water over the face) or with adenosine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Atrial fibrillation (Choice A) can occur with a rapid ventricular rate but typically presents with irregular tachycardia. Atrial fibrillation also occurs more often in patients with structural heart disease, and supraventricular tachycardia is more likely in a previously healthy patient with regular tachycardia. Long QT interval syndrome (Choice B) is a disorder of prolonged ventricular depolarization and repolarization. It appears on ECG with a prolonged QT interval. It can be complicated by polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or torsades de pointes. Sinus tachycardia (Choice C) would be unlikely to have a pulse of 260/min. The maximal pulse from the sinus node is typically lower than 220/min and on ECG, there are P waves prior to every QRS complex. Pulse resulting from supraventricular tachycardia can be higher because of a reentrant rhythm that bypasses the atrioventricular node. Ventricular tachycardia (VT) (Choice E) shows a wide QRS complex tachycardia on ECG. VT occurs when an abnormal electrical focus or a reentry circuit causes rapid contraction of the ventricles. There are many criteria for defining VT on the rhythm strip, but the general morphology will show wide QRS complex tachycardia. There are monomorphic and polymorphic forms of VT. Treatment depends on the duration, type, and symptomatology. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to an abnormally rapid pulse and rhythm originating from above the ventricles, typically with a narrow QRS complex on ECG. II

questionStem: A previously healthy 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 2-month history of the left eye wandering . She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Examination of the eye shows left eye wandering . A photograph of the eyes is shown . The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This child presents with leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex) and a sensory exotropia, which is suggestive of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of retinal neuroendocrine cells and is the most common ophthalmic malignancy in children. Retinoblastoma results from inactivating mutations of both copies of the RB1 gene, which functions as a tumor suppressor by halting cell cycle progression at the G1 checkpoint. RB1 mutations may be either acquired or inherited. In cases of germline RB1 mutation, a single mutated allele is inherited, and the second allele acquires a subsequent mutation during development. Infants who carry germline mutations are more likely to have bilateral retinoblastoma with multiple foci of tumors in the eye, whereas infants with two acquired mutations are more likely to have unilateral retinoblastoma. Ultrasound of the eye is helpful for defining the size of the lesion and for detecting characteristic intralesional calcifications. Within the eye, large tumor size, tumor seeding of the vitreous humor, and involvement of the iris or anterior chamber are associated with a worse prognosis. If undetected, retinoblastoma may invade the optic nerve, leading to a greater risk for metastasis to the brain. Most cases of retinoblastoma may be successfully managed with chemotherapy, although advanced cases may require enucleation with special attention paid to achieving negative margins at the optic nerve, as cases that have undergone metastasis have a poor prognosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acquired exotropia (Choice A) may result from visual sensory deprivation in a non-seeing eye. However, exotropia will not cause leukocoria. Chronic endophthalmitis (Choice B) typically results from hematogenous spread of bacteria or fungus or following ocular surgery. This infant is not ill­ appearing and lacks a history suggestive of a likely cause of endophthalmitis. Eyes affected by endophthalmitis are often painful and have conjunctiva! injection. Congenital glaucoma (Choice C) presents with characteristic findings including buphthalmos (an enlarged eye), a large cornea, which may be edematous and opacified, and increased intraocular pressure. Infants typically present with epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm or eye rubbing. Congenital glaucoma does not cause leukocoria. Familial cataract (Choice D) may be either unilateral or bilateral and may be associated with chromosomal abnormalities or inherited mutations in a variety of genes. Congenital cataracts are present at birth. This child has developed a wandering eye after normal development for the first several months of life, which is more consistent with a diagnosis of retinoblastoma. Educational Objective: Leukocoria in an infant raises concern for retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of retinal neuroendocrine cells and is the most common ophthalmic malignancy in children. It results from biallelic, inherited or acquired, inactivating mutations of the RB1 gene, a tumor suppressor. Treatment is with chemotherapy or enucleation.

questionStem: A 10-year-old boy develops a rash on the chest 2 days after returning from a beach vacation . Over the next 2 weeks , the lesions spread to the back, abdomen , and extremities . There are multiple well-demarcated papules and small, thin, round plaques covered with fine white scales over the torso and extremities . Removal of a scale causes minor bleeding at the site. There is pitting of the fingernails . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Guttate psoriasis is characterized by numerous papules and small plaques scattered all over the trunk and extremities. Each individual papule or plaque has a small amount of white scale over the top. Like psoriasis vulgaris, removal of the white scale causes pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign). This is because of the thinning of the epidermis over the dermal capillaries, which are also dilated in psoriasis. Removal of the scales also causes Koebner phenomenon, the development of new lesions at sites of trauma. All forms of psoriasis, including guttate psoriasis, may be accompanied by nail changes. The most common nail change in psoriasis is pitting, which is seen in this patient, but onycholysis (splitting of the nail plate from the nail bed) is also common. Presence or absence of nail involvement is a useful physical examination consideration when evaluating any full body rash. Guttate psoriasis is often triggered by a streptococcal infection or by medications, though neither of these triggers are relevant in this case. Treatment of guttate psoriasis includes topical therapies such as corticosteroids and vitamin D analogs. If the psoriasis is refractory to topical therapies, then phototherapy, methotrexate, or biologic medications may be considered.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cellulitis (Choice A) presents with cutaneous pain, erythema, and induration spreading outward from a source of infection, often an initial abrasion or injection. The numerous papules and small plaques seen in this case are characteristic of guttate psoriasis, not cellulitis. However, a streptococcal cellulitis could potentially trigger guttate psoriasis. Nummular eczema (Choice B) is a term used to describe eczematous patches which are round or coin shaped. Like other forms of eczema, or dermatitis, the rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting. With chronic scratching, the affected areas become dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. Pityriasis rosea (Choice C) is a cutaneous eruption characterized by the acute onset of a pruritic patch, which is followed by the development of numerous smaller macules and patches. It commonly involves the trunk and proximal extremities. It is usually induced by a viral infection including human herpesvirus 6 and 7, though often the exact infection is not determined. In this case, a pruritic patch was not seen making guttate psoriasis more likely than pityriasis rosea. Tinea corporis (Choice E) is caused by a superficial dermatophyte infection of the skin, most often Trichophyton tonsurans. The classic appearance is a round, annular patch with a scaly border. Potassium hydroxide preparation will show hyphae. Numerous small papules and plaques are not typically seen. Educational Objective: Guttate psoriasis is a form of psoriasis in which small, scaly papules and plaques develop diffusely over the trunk and extremities. It is often triggered by a streptococcal infection. Nail pitting and onycholysis may be seen in all types of psoriasis, including guttate.

questionStem: A previously healthy 13-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the acute onset of mild difficulty breathing and a persistent , nonproductive cough . He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. Immunizations are up-to-date . On arrival , he is alert but in mild respiratory distress . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 85/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Examination shows no nasal discharge or stridor. Expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally, but they are greater on the right. His symptoms do not improve following treatment with nebulized albuterol. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung but no infiltrate or foreign body. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.E: Endoscopic examination of the patient's airway

correctExplanation: Wheezing that does not improve with nebulized albuterol, hyperinflation of the right lung, and acute onset of difficulty breathing and cough raises suspicion for foreign body aspiration. Foreign body aspiration can cause obstruction of the airway, leading to impaired oxygenation and ventilation. Children from 1 to 3 years old are at increased risk for foreign body aspiration because of their ability to stand and mobilize independently, ability to grasp and put small objects into their mouths, and an immature swallowing mechanism. Foreign bodies can be located anywhere in the airway between the larynx and the bronchi. Children can present with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, and stridor, or may have a less severe presentation with partial airway obstruction, presenting with cough, tachypnea, decreased air entry on auscultation, or wheezing. Chest x-ray can show hyperinflation of one lung, which is caused by air trapping and partial airway obstruction in which air is able to pass via inspiration, but not exhalation. Foreign bodies are typically in the right lung because of the more vertical anatomic position of the right main bronchus. Management of foreign body aspiration involves flexible or rigid bronchoscopy to remove the object. Object removal is necessary and retained foreign bodies can be complicated by airway inflammation and infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Chest percussion and physiotherapy (Choice A) can be beneficial for patients with mucus plugging of small airways, such as in cystic fibrosis. Chest percussion can help dislodge mucus and improve its clearance by coughing. Oral administration of amoxicillin (Choice B) would be indicated if the patient presented with a bacterial illness, such as pneumonia, streptococcal pharyngitis, or acute otitis media. Patients with pneumonia can also present with cough, however it is typically a subacute onset and a chest x-ray would show localized infiltrate or opacification in an area of the lung. Oral administration of corticosteroids (Choice C) would be helpful in a patient with moderate to severe acute asthma exacerbation along with nebulized albuterol. Corticosteroids reduce inflammation of airways and have been shown to decrease hospitalizations for asthma. This patient's wheezing did not improve with nebulized albuterol, making acute asthma exacerbation less likely. Subcutaneous administration of epinephrine (Choice D) would not be indicated in this patient. Intramuscular epinephrine is used in the emergent treatment of anaphylaxis, which can be characterized by urticaria, vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing, stridor, oropharyngeal swelling, and airway obstruction. However, this patient's wheezing is more likely caused by foreign body aspiration and the patient has no other signs of anaphylaxis. Furthermore, intramuscular epinephrine is preferred over subcutaneous administration because of its more rapid and reliable onset. Educational Objective: Children with foreign body aspiration can present with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, and stridor, or they may have a less severe presentation with cough, tachypnea, decreased air entry on auscultation, or wheezing caused by a partial airway obstruction.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy has had pain in the groin and thigh for 2 weeks ; 1 week ago , he began limping . There is no history of recent febrile illness . X-rays of the hips show normal findings . A bone scan shows decreased uptake in the right hip. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease refers to idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head that most commonly occurs in younger boys aged 4 to 9 years. The classic presentation includes slow onset of hip pain which is worsened by activity and associated with a limp. The pain may or may not be relieved with rest. X-rays often show no abnormalities. However, bone scan characteristically shows decreased perfusion of the femoral head, as in this case. MRI may also be considered for diagnosis and will show bone marrow changes. Treatments include preventing weight-bearing on the affected leg and, occasionally, may require operative intervention or hip arthroplasty. Inadequate treatment results in fragmentation and subsequent deformity of the femoral head.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Ankylosing spondylitis (Choice A) is a rheumatologic inflammatory condition involving the vertebrae that presents with subacute to chronic back pain and limited range of motion that is improved with exercise. The resultant arthropathy can result in frequent falls and fractures, however without back pain or any systemic inflammatory manifestations, it would be an unlikely diagnosis in this case. Pauciarticular juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Choice C), also called oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, is most common in girls aged 2 to 3 years. It presents with swelling of a single joint, often the knee, with accompanied limping but no pain. On examination, the involved joints are swollen and tender without erythema. Unlike other forms of juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic manifestations are characteristically absent. Septic arthritis (Choice D) results from bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically shows purulent synovial fluid with greater than 50,000 leukocytes per mm 3. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (Choice E) most commonly occurs in overweight children between the ages of 10 to 15 years. It results in displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck secondary to anterosuperior movement of the metaphysis caused by a fracture of the growth plate. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Choice F) is an autoimmune disease resulting in a constellation of symptoms including fever, rash, photosensitivity, renal disease, and nonerosive arthritis. It is more common in female patients and isolated monoarticular joint involvement is inadequate for diagnosis. Toxic synovitis (Choice G), also known as transient synovitis, is a non-infectious arthropathy that presents with pain in a joint, often the hip, frequently following a viral infection in a child. It is unlikely in this child who has not had any recent illness and has decreased uptake on bone scan. Educational Objective: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease refers to idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, which typically presents in young boys with a limp and hip pain. It requires early recognition and intervention to prevent long-term deformity.

questionStem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 1-day history of fever and poor feeding . She vomited once 6 hours ago, and her parents have noticed several lesions on her skin since then . They say she has been sleepy and has not been acting like herself . She has not had diarrhea . She was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. She is at the 25th percentile for length, weight , and head circumference . Her temperature is 38°C (100.4 °F), pulse is 180/min, respirations are 40/min , and blood pressure is 63/45 mm Hg. Examination shows 3- to 8-mm , nonblanching , erythematous lesions over the scalp, trunk , and proximal upper and lower extremities . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Serum studies show: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows : 136 mEq/L 3.6 mEq/L 100 mEq/L 17 mEq/L pH 7.32 Pco2 38 mm Hg Po2 94 mm Hg In addition to administration of intravenous antibiotics , which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Meningitis in infants is commonly caused by bacteria and can present with fever or hypothermia, lethargy, irritability, altered mental status, a bulging fontanelle, poor feeding, and seizures. Diagnosis of meningitis typically involves lumbar puncture, and evaluation of the cerebrospinal fluid will show an increased white blood cell count with predominant neutrophils, increased protein, and decreased glucose. Thorough evaluation also includes a complete blood count, blood culture, and urine culture to evaluate for other causes of sepsis, as well as culture of the cerebrospinal fluid to determine the causative organism. This patient has signs of sepsis, a systemic inflammatory syndrome that may occur in response to infection. Sepsis can be complicated by shock and multiorgan failure with a high mortality rate. Septic shock is characterized by vasoplegia (impaired response of the vasculature to vasoconstricting stimuli) with markedly decreased systemic vascular resistance, tachycardia, increased cardiac output, oliguria, and lactic acidosis. The initial step for management in septic shock involves emergency antibiotics and fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids, such as 0.9% saline.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Administration of dopamine (Choice A) or epinephrine (Choice B) may be indicated in this patient if the patient continues to be hypotensive after a trial of fluid resuscitation. Fluid administration should be the initial step for resuscitation of septic shock. Administration of sodium bicarbonate (Choice D) would be unlikely to be beneficial in this patient, as this patient's pH is normal. Administration of sodium bicarbonate may be helpful in patients who are acidotic. Endotracheal intubation (Choice E) would not be emergently indicated in this patient as the patient is breathing, ventilating, and oxygenating well as shown on arterial blood gas analysis. The patient's hypotension and hemodynamic instability would also cause increased risk for cardiac arrest if endotracheal intubation were attempted. Educational Objective: Sepsis can be complicated by shock, hypotension, and multiorgan failure with an increased mortality rate. The initial step for management in septic shock involves emergent antibiotics and fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids, such as 0.9% saline.

questionStem: A 4-year-old African American girl has pallor and progressive malaise 6 weeks after being diagnosed with severe hepatitis A. Examination 4 weeks after diagnosis showed improvement in symptoms . She now has scattered petechiae and ecchymoses . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Reticulocyte count Platelet count Serum iron A blood smear shows normochromic , normocytic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: 6.5 g/dL 82 µm3 2100/mm 3 1.0% 21 ,000/mm 3 250 µg/dL Aplastic anemia (AA) is the most likely cause of this patient's normocytic anemia , leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia with normal serum iron following infection with hepatitis A. AA can either be inherited or acquired . Acquired AA may follow exposure to certain types of viruses (eg, hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus, or HIV), chemicals (eg, benzene), or medications (eg, methimazole, sulfa antibiotics, or chloramphenicol), or it may be idiopathic. The method of bone marrow progenitor destruction is thought to be autoimmune. Patients who develop AA after a viral infection usually present with pancytopenia within 6 months after diagnosis, but symptoms related to pancytopenia such as fatigue, exercise intolerance , pallor, and petechiae, often appear sooner. Diagnosis includes bone marrow biopsy and aspiration, which will show a profoundly hypocellular bone marrow with a paucity of progenitor cells of all lineages with replacement by fat and stroma. Importantly, malignant cells and fibrosis will be absent. Treatment is either with immunosuppressive medications or hematopoietic stem cell transplant from a matched sibling if available .
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Anemia, acute hemorrhagic, (Choice A) describes massive blood loss that leads to anemia. This is common in trauma and presents with anemia in the absence of leukopenia or thrombocytopenia . Anemia, autoimmune hemolytic (Choice C), results from the binding of an autoantibody to red blood cell surface antigens, leading to removal via the reticuloendothelial system or to intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis is made by a positive Coombs test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, decreased haptoglobin, and the presence of spherocytes and reticulocytes on the peripheral smear. Anemia, chronic disease (Choice D), is a common finding in autoimmune and inflammatory disease, chronic infections, and malignancy. Increased hepcidin concentrations decrease iron absorption and increase iron storage in the bone marrow, preventing use of iron by erythrocyte precursors and resulting in anemia. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (Choice E) results in hemolysis upon exposure to certain medications such as sulfa drugs and oxidants. It does not cause marked leukopenia or thrombocytopenia.

questionStem: A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after a PPD skin test produced 17 mm of induration at 48 hours. She takes no medications . She drinks alcohol and smokes cigarettes and marijuana occasionally . She is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently for contraception . She lives in a rural community , and she raises chickens and cows. She participates in the student government and volunteers at a skilled nursing care facility. She traveled to Ireland for 10 days last summer with her high school. Examination shows no additional abnormalities . Which of the following activities is the strongest predisposing factor for this patient's positive PPD skin test?

choices.F: Volunteering at a skilled nursing care facility

correctExplanation: lnduration exceeding 15 mm is considered a positive result for a PPD skin test and is suggestive of latent tuberculosis infection in this patient. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing mycobacterial organism transmitted via respiratory secretions. It presents with primary, latent, and reactivation patterns. In primary disease, patients present with subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. Latent tuberculosis can occur as the organism proliferates within macrophages and is maintained within caseating granulomas. PPD skin testing stimulates a T-lymphocyte driven type IV hypersensitivity reaction against subdermal tuberculin antigen. Causes of false positive PPD testing include prior vaccination with Bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccine. This patient's positive test result likely represents a true positive. Her most significant risk factor for tuberculosis is volunteering in a skilled nursing care facility, as tuberculosis is more common and spreads more easily in crowded populations, such as in nursing facilities and prisons . Latent tuberculosis is treated with a prolonged course of isoniazid or rifampin.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. While overseas travel (Choice A) to endemic areas is a significant risk factor for tuberculosis, Ireland and western Europe are not endemic areas for tuberculosis. Endemic regions for tuberculosis include sub-Saharan Africa, the Indian subcontinent, and eastern and southeastern Asia. Participation in high school events (Choice B) is not a significant risk factor for tuberculosis. Prolonged conditions of crowding, as in a prison, are a more significant risk factor for tuberculosis than single large events, which do not confer significant risk in non-endemic areas. Raising livestock (Choice C) confers increased risk for acquiring particular infectious organisms, such as Bacillus anthracis, Coxiel/a burnetii, and Francisel/a tularensis. M. tuberculosis is not a zoonotic organism and is spread by human-to-human contact. Sexual activity (Choice D) does not confer an increased risk for acquiring tuberculosis. M. tuberculosis is not a sexually transmitted organism and is spread by respiratory secretions. Smoking marijuana (Choice E) does not confer an increased risk for acquiring tuberculosis. While chronic pulmonary disease, such as silicosis, does confer an increased risk for tuberculosis, this is unlikely in a teenage patient with occasional marijuana use. Educational Objective: lnduration exceeding 15 mm is considered a positive result for a PPD skin test. Risk factors for tuberculosis include exposure to crowded conditions, as in a skilled nursing care facility or prison, residence or travel in an endemic area, and causes of immunocompromise, such as diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, or HIV infection.

questionStem: A 7-year-old girl is brought for a follow-up examination 2 days after completing a 10-day course of antibiotics for her second episode of pneumococcal pneumonia during the past year ; during this time, she has also had two episodes of otitis media and one episode of herpes zoster. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and was healthy until 1 year ago when she began to have frequent upper and lower respiratory tract infections . Her mother was recently hospitalized for treatment of nontuberculous mycobacterial bacteremia . Examination of the patient shows 2-cm nontender lymph nodes in the axillae . There is fluid behind both tympanic membranes . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: HIV infection, acquired via vertical transmission from the patient's mother, is the most likely cause of the patient's recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia, otitis media, and herpes zoster infection with axillary lymphadenopathy. HIV transmission may occur at any time during gestation but is most commonly acquired at or around the time of delivery and in the immediate postpartum period during breastfeeding. Transmission is uncommon if the mother is taking antiretroviral therapy and has a decreased HIV viral load. As a result of screening for HIV in most developed countries, the incidence of perinatal and pediatric HIV infection has decreased, although this is not true around the world. While many pediatric patients with perinatally acquired HIV infection will manifest symptoms within the first few months to years, it has been recognized that a subpopulation of patients will not develop symptoms or AIDS-defining conditions until many years later, as in this case. Symptoms in children are non-specific, and AIDS-defining conditions in children younger than six vary slightly from those in older children and adults. Clues to the diagnosis in this case include the presence of nontuberculous mycobacterial infection in the patient's mother, which is an AIDS-defining illness and should prompt evaluation for HIV infection in this patient.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chronic granulomatous disease (Choice A) is caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency and results in impaired intracellular killing of catalase positive pathogens. Streptococcus pneumoniae is catalase negative. Patients present with recurrent pyogenic infections with organisms such as S. aureus. Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome (Choice C) is caused by mutations in the JAK-STAT signaling cascade, which impairs the development and function of T helper 17 (Th n) cells. Th 17 cells secrete interleukin-17 (IL-17), a potent neutrophil chemotaxis agent, so deficiency results in poor neutrophil migration to sites of infection. Patients have recurrent skin infections but with non-inflamed abscesses (cold abscess) and diffuse atopic dermatitis. Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) (Choice D) is caused by a 22q11 deletion that leads to failure of the third and fourth branchial pouches to develop. These structures give rise to the thymus and parathyroid glands, and their absence leads to thymic aplasia and hypocalcemia in cardiac and craniofacial defects. Patients are susceptible to viral and fungal infections. X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Choice E) occurs as a result of mutations in the BTK gene that encodes a tyrosine kinase essential for all stages of B-lymphocyte development and proliferation. Patients lack functioning B lymphocytes, and therefore, lack normal concentrations of immunoglobulins. It nearly always presents within the first eighteen months of life with recurrent infections. It is more common in male patients given X-linked inheritance. Educational Objective: Pediatric HIV/AIDS infection should be suspected in patients who present with recurrent bacterial pneumonia or AIDS-defining illnesses such as disseminated mycobacterial and non­ mycobacterial infection or Pneumocystis jiroveci infection.

questionStem: A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea for 6 hours. He and his family recently immigrated to the USA from Mexico. Abdominal examination shows pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. There is mild hepatomegaly . Sigmoidoscopy with mucosal biopsy shows flask-shaped ulcers with healthy intervening mucosa . Which of the following is the most likely pathogen?
correctExplanation: Infection with En/amoeba histolytica leads to amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery). Amoebiasis is much more common in the developing world. E. histolytica is an amoebic parasite and forms cysts which can be transmitted through the fecal oral route and through ingestion of contaminated water. Amoebic cysts mature to trophozoites in the large bowel. Trophozoites may invade the colonic mucosa and interstitium, leading to symptoms of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Invasive infections can lead to colonic perforation and sepsis. If trophozoites enter the bloodstream, they may travel to the liver and cause hepatic amoebic abscesses, which present with fever and right upper quadrant pain. Diagnosis can be made with identification of cysts on stool microscopy or peripheral smear, which may show trophozoites with endosomes containing red blood cells, as well as by antibody assay or polymerase chain reaction testing. Colonoscopy shows mucosal ulcers that are often flask shaped. Treatment requires combination therapy with metronidazole or linidazole as well as an anti-luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Giardia lamblia (Choice B) is a parasitic organism that causes giardiasis. Light microscopy shows a pear-shaped, binucleate, flagellated trophozoite. Parasitic overgrowth of the small bowel leads to intestinal malabsorption. While the diarrhea associated with giardiasis may occasionally be bloody, this symptom is less frequently observed than malabsorption. Rotavirus (Choice C) is a double-stranded RNA virus that causes infectious diarrhea in children. The diarrhea caused by rotavirus is watery, profuse, and often foul-smelling; ii is typically not bloody. Salmonella typhi (Choice D) is a Gram-negative, encapsulated, facultative anaerobic bacillus that causes infectious diarrhea and typhoid fever, which presents with fever, abdominal pain, rash, and diarrhea. S. typhi does not typically cause focal right upper quadrant pain or bloody diarrhea. Shigella sonnei (Choice E) is a Gram-negative bacillus that causes shigellosis, which presents with bloody diarrhea, and which may cause hemolytic uremic syndrome. S. sonnei does not cause focal right upper quadrant pain, which is suggestive of hepatic abscess. Educational Objective: E. histolytica is an amoebic parasite that causes intestinal amoebiasis, which presents with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Extracolonic invasion of the bloodstream may occur, leading to the formation of hepatic abscesses that present with fever and right upper quadrant pain. Treatment requires combination therapy with metronidazole or linidazole along with an anti-luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol.

questionStem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he fell approximately 8 feet from a backyard porch onto a firm dirt surface , landing on his back. On arrival, he appears mildly uncomfortable . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 85/55 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate right-sided flank tenderness . The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is measurement of which of the following?
correctExplanation: This patient's fall from a height and subsequent left flank tenderness raises concern for blunt kidney trauma. Motor vehicle collisions, falls, and sports injuries are common causes of this type of injury. A rapid deceleration injury, such as caused by a fall, can cause the kidney to be crushed against the paravertebral muscles, avulsed from the ureteropelvic junction or the renal vessels, or thrombosed. In any of these cases, blood supply to the kidney is interrupted. Flank tenderness, flank bruising, or lower rib fractures should all raise concern for blunt kidney injury. Hematuria is a common presenting symptom seen in over two-thirds of patients with blunt renal injury. It should be investigated quickly with measurement of urine blood as part of the initial trauma assessment, as intravenous fluid administration can dilute hematuria and preclude detection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Serum creatinine (Choice A) and urea nitrogen (Choice B) are not helpful in diagnosing acute blunt kidney trauma. Any abnormality in renal function caused by trauma is masked by the contralateral functioning kidney. Therefore, neither creatinine nor urea nitrogen may be used as an indicator of renal trauma. Urine protein (Choice D) and volume (Choice E) may also be normal after blunt kidney trauma. They are not helpful in identifying the presence or absence of traumatic kidney injury. These values may later change if the filtering capacity of the kidney is impaired, but they are not useful in the initial trauma assessment. Educational Objective: Blunt kidney trauma is caused by rapid deceleration, such as a fall from a height. Evaluating for hematuria should be included in the initial trauma assessment and is the best indicator of kidney trauma.

questionStem: A 4-month-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of severe coughing for 2 days . The cough is episodic and staccato-like and often followed by vomiting . One week ago, she developed rhinorrhea . On admission , she appears well when not coughing . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 34/min . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. Examination shows a few petechiae on the face and thick nasal secretions . An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to prevent nosocomial transmission?

choices.A: Antiviral therapy for all health care workers
choices.D: Erythromycin therapy for all health care workers
choices.E: Intravenous immune globulin therapy for all health care workers
choices.F: Intravenous immune globulin therapy for the patient
choices.G: Pertussis vaccination for all health care workers

correctExplanation: Droplet isolation or droplet precautions, in which the eyes, nose, and mouth are covered by glasses and a mask, would be the most effective way to prevent nosocomial spread of 8ordetella pertussis, an infection characterized by episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing and post-tussive emesis. Pertussis classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, pneumothorax, and facial petechiae. Often, such coughing fits are accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve during the convalescent stage, which lasts from 1 to 4 weeks. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization in the form of acellular pertussis, typically administered along with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines (DTaP). It can be transmitted in respiratory droplets, thus all individuals who come into contact with infected patients should wear a mask and eye protection.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Antiviral therapy for all health care workers {Choice A) can be given with oseltamivir in an influenza outbreak, but 8. pertussis is a bacterial infection and would not be treated with an antiviral medication. Contact isolation {Choice B) is reserved for pathogens such as C/ostridium difficile, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and others that are easily transmitted through contact with the skin. These precautions involve the wearing of disposable gloves and gowns. Erythromycin therapy for all healthcare workers {Choice D) could be considered in instances of a 8. pertussis outbreak, which can occur if the index case is not recognized or droplet precautions are not instituted but is not necessary in this case. Intravenous immune globulin therapy for all health care workers {Choice E) is not used for post-exposure prophylaxis for 8. pertussis. Intravenous immune globulin therapy for patients {Choice F) is occasionally given after exposure to certain pathogens. For example, those exposed to rabies are given both rabies immune globulin and a rabies vaccine. Pertussis vaccination for all healthcare workers {Choice G) is not correct. While all adults should receive the tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis vaccine {Tdap) every 10 years, infection can occur even in patients who have recently been vaccinated. The best method of preventing infection is the use of droplet precautions. Pertussis vaccination for the patient {Choice H) will not change her disease course, although vaccination is still recommended at 4 months, 6 months, 15 months, and at age 4.

questionStem: An 11-year-old girl with spina bifida is brought to the physician because of right thigh pain for 2 days . She is paraplegic and has limited sensation below the waist. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 95/min , and respirations are 16/min. Examination shows swelling of the right distal thigh without redness . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: This patient's presentation with distal thigh swelling is concerning for a fracture of the diaphysis of the femur. Femoral fractures are a common long bone fracture in children, with peaks of incidence in toddlers because of accidental trauma and adolescents because of motor vehicle collisions. A femoral shaft fracture may be complicated by shortening of the muscles of the knee and hip which causes the fractured femur to displace, so early recognition and intervention is needed to prevent permanent limb length discrepancy. Clinically, most femoral shaft fractures will demonstrate obvious deformity, swelling, shortening, or crepitus on examination. A neurovascular examination distal to the site of swelling should be performed to ensure that the fracture has not caused damage to nerves or arteries. The next step in management of a suspected femoral fracture is radiographic assessment using standard anterior-posterior and lateral plain x-rays of the affected area and the joints above and below the suspected fracture. This ensures correct diagnosis and assists in management planning.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reassurance (Choice A) and application of local heat (Choice B) are not appropriate in this case as the suspected femoral fracture will need to be immobilized and may require operative intervention. In cases of mild musculoskeletal injuries that do not require medical evaluation, application of ice is more effective than application of heat. Range of motion exercises (Choice D) may be needed following complete healing of the femoral fracture, but if performed now without adequate treatment, they would likely worsen the fracture. Immobilization is an important step in treatment of a femoral fracture. Acetaminophen therapy (Choice E) may be used for mild musculoskeletal complaints and is safe for use in children. However, treating pain without addressing the underlying cause, such as a fracture, is not appropriate. Educational Objective: When a fracture is suspected, the next step in management is radiographic assessment of the affected area and the joints above and below it.

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not had a menstrual period for 4 months. Menarche was at the age of 12 years ; menses previously occurred at regular 30-day intervals . She also reports increased hair growth between her breasts and on her chin as well as acne on her forehead and nose. She had sexual intercourse for the first time at the age of 14 years ; she most recently had sexual intercourse 5 months ago. She and her partners have used condoms consistently . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 84 kg (185 lb); BMI is 32 kg/m 2• Physical examination shows coarse hair over the chin and dark, velvety skin over the back of the neck. There are numerous papules and pustules over the face. The abdomen is obese , soft, and nontender ; there are no masses . Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 5. A pregnancy test is negative . Which of the following is the most likely location of the pathology causing this patient's symptoms?
correctExplanation: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) presents with irregular menses, infertility, hirsutism, and acne, often in patients with an increased body weight. It requires two of the following for diagnosis: oligo- or anovulation, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, and clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (eg, hirsutism, acne). It is also associated with signs of insulin resistance, such as acanthosis nigricans and increased blood glucose concentrations. PCOS is caused by an abnormal hypothalamic hormonal feedback response, that is caused by a primary functional ovarian hyperandrogenism (increased androgens produced by the theca lutein cells), which leads to increased luteinizing hormone (LH) in comparison to follicle stimulating hormone (FSH). Treatment includes weight loss, combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, and spironolactone or ketoconazole for hirsutism. Clomiphene stimulates increased ovulation and can also be utilized for individuals desiring pregnancy as can metformin. If the patient is diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, oral antihyperglycemic medications or insulin may also be necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hypothalamus (Choice A) pathologies can lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which can lead to primary or secondary amenorrhea caused by anovulation.
