Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is more commonly seen in young, athletic, thin female patients and would be less likely in this obese patient with hirsutism. Pancreas (Choice C) pathologies include insulinomas and glucagonomas. lnsulinomas are tumors of the pancreatic ~ cells that present with hypoglycemia, whereas glucagonomas are tumors of the a cells that present with increased blood glucose concentrations, polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Neither present with hirsutism. Pituitary gland (Choice D) pathologies can also lead to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which presents with anovulation and menstrual irregularities, as well as deficiencies in growth hormone, leading to short stature, and prolactin. Thyroid gland (Choice E) pathologies include hypo- and hyperthyroidism, both of which can present with anovulation and menstrual irregularities. Hyperthyroidism presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss, diaphoresis, and diarrhea. Hypothyroidism presents with weight gain, fatigue, constipation, and cold intolerance. This patient does not have any symptoms to suggest a thyroid pathology. Educational Objective: Polycystic ovary syndrome presents with menstrual irregularities, signs of androgen excess, obesity, insulin resistance, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Treatment includes weight loss and combined oral contraceptives for menstrual regulation, and antihyperglycemic medications or insulin for the management of diabetes mellitus, if diagnosed.

questionStem: An asymptomatic 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He is concerned because he is the shortest student in his class . Review of his records from the age of 8 years to today shows a consistent pattern of height at the 3rd percentile and weight at the 25th percentile . He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . His last routine examination 2 years ago showed no abnormalities . His mother is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall, and his father is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall. He says his parents are always nagging him to eat better, but he thinks his diet is okay. Genital and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 2. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's short stature?
correctExplanation: This patient's most likely diagnosis is constitutional growth delay, which is a normal variant of growth. Short stature has a variety of causes, such as constitutional growth delay, familial (hereditary) short stature, chronic steroid use, endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency), cardiopulmonary disease, and genetic disorders (eg, Down syndrome, Turner syndrome). Familial short stature and constitutional growth delay are the most common causes of short stature. Familial short stature is associated with short stature in both parents, a normal gain of height velocity, and a bone age that corresponds with chronological age, whereas a constitutional growth delay is independent of parental stature, has a consistently decreased growth velocity, and has a bone age younger than chronological age. Patients with constitutional growth delay may experience a delayed onset of puberty. These patients typically reach a normal adult height, with more rapid increases in height gain velocity as they progress through puberty. This patient has parents with normal stature and a decreased growth velocity, leading to a height that is consistently in the 3rd percentile. He does not have other signs or symptoms to suggest a pathologic cause of short stature, making constitutional growth delay the most likely diagnosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A) typically presents with fatigue, nausea, fasting hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, and morning headache caused by glucocorticoid insufficiency. Patients with primary adrenal insufficiency may also demonstrate mineralocorticoid and androgen deficiency, which would present with urinary salt wasting and decreased body hair, respectively. This patient does not demonstrate the symptoms or physical examination signs of adrenal insufficiency. Familial short stature (Choice C) typically presents in young patients whose parents are both of short stature with a normal growth velocity and bone age consistent with chronological age. These patients will remain of short stature into adulthood. This patient has parents with normal stature, making this answer less likely. Growth hormone deficiency (Choice D) is a rare condition that can present in infancy or childhood depending on the severity of deficiency. Acquired growth hormone deficiency is typically caused by a non-functional pituitary tumor and presents with severe growth delay and a bone age younger than chronological age. It is associated with a rapid decline in the height-for-age curve, crossing percentiles. This patient's growth velocity has been slow but consistent, making growth hormone deficiency a less likely cause of his short stature. Insufficient caloric intake (Choice E) typically results in an abnormally low weight along with signs of malnutrition such as dry skin and hair loss (caused by decreased protein stores). This patient has a normal weight and lacks physical examination signs of malnutrition. Educational Objective: Constitutional growth delay is a normal growth variant that occurs in patients with parents of normal stature. Patients typically present with short stature, delayed pubertal development, slow but consistent growth velocity, and a bone age less than chronological age. It is associated with normal development and stature once the patient reaches puberty.

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of clumsiness and frequent falls over the past 6 months . He did not walk independently until 17 months of age and has always had poor motor skills. There is enlargement of the calf muscles and a positive Gowers sign. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern?
correctExplanation: X-linked recessive is the mode of inheritance for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy typically have an unremarkable birth history, then begin to demonstrate signs of proximal muscle weakness early in childhood. Physical examination discloses difficulty rising from squatting position, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a Gower sign (using hands to "climb" up the lower extremities when rising from the floor). Proximal muscles include those of the shoulder and hip girdles, such as the adductors and flexors of the hip and thigh. Muscle biopsy used to be a mainstay of diagnosis, but genetic testing has rendered this largely unnecessary. Most affected patients will require the use of a wheelchair by early adolescence. Additional late findings include dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure, which may be the cause of death in these patients.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Autosomal dominant (Choice A) and autosomal recessive (Choice B) are not the inheritance patterns of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, although either one can be the inheritance pattern of Limb-Girdle muscular dystrophy, which is characterized by shoulder and pelvic girdle weakness with normal distal muscle strength. X-linked dominant (Choice C) is the inheritance pattern of scapuloperoneal myopathy, which presents with weakness of the distal leg and scapula. Facial muscles are occasionally affected. X-linked dominant differs from X-linked recessive in that only a single copy is required for expression of the disease phenotype, even in females, who have two X-chromosomes. No known mendelian pattern (Choice E) is not the correct answer. Many of the muscular dystrophies are inherited in a mendelian pattern, although inflammatory and infectious myopathies occur sporadically and are not genetically determined. Educational Objective: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive condition, results in progressive proximal muscle weakness after a period of relatively normal development. Symptoms include an inability to rise from a squatting position and weakness of the lower limb girdle. Late complications include dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory insufficiency.

questionStem: A 1-month-old boy is brought for a well-child examination . He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy . Fifteen minutes after delivery, a very soft systolic murmur was heard along the left sternal border. He appears well today. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 76/54 mm Hg. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the middle left sternal border. Examination shows no other abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely physiologic mechanism for the change in intensity of this patient's murmur?
correctExplanation: Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance most likely explains the increased intensity of this patient's holosystolic murmur, which is consistent with a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Normal fetal circulation is unique in that oxygenated blood arrives from the maternal circulation via the umbilical vein and reaches the inferior vena cava. From there, oxygenated blood is shunted from the right atrium to the left atrium, left ventricle {LV), and systemic circulation. The fetal lungs are filled with amniotic fluid while in utero, so the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high. In patients with a VSD, increased PVR effectively prevents left-to-right shunting of blood from the LV to the right ventricle (RV). At birth, amniotic fluid is cleared and expelled from the lungs and the PVR decreases dramatically, followed by a gradual decrease in PVR over the next several weeks. As the PVR decreases, the pressure gradient between the LV and the RV increases such that blood is shunted from the LV to the RV with each cardiac cycle. This change in PVR explains the change in the patient's murmur.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Closed ductus arteriosus (DA) {Choice A) is a normal finding in newborns and occurs within several days of delivery. Continued patency of the DA leads to a continuous murmur, not a holosystolic murmur. Improved atrial natriuretic factor functioning {Choice C) is not the answer. This is a substance that is released by atria in response to increases in circulating volume to induce natriuresis in the kidneys. It does not explain the change in this patient's murmur. Improved myocardial contractility {Choice D) would not explain the change in the murmur as increased contractility would likely be equal between the two ventricles, with little to no change in the pressure gradient between the two. Increased circulating blood volume {Choice E) is incorrect. VSDs that are large enough to cause right ventricular overload may manifest later in life with evidence of right heart failure and volume overload. Educational Objective: In the fetal circulation, increased PVR prevents a left-to-right shunt from the LV to the RV through a VSD. At the time of birth, the rapid decrease in PVR creates a substantial pressure gradient between the two ventricles and allows for the development of a left-to-right shunt. The PVR continues to drop over the following weeks and likely accounts for the change in this patient's murmur.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of eye swelling for 1 week . His blood pressure is 120/60 mm Hg. Examination shows generalized edema and ascites. Serum studies show a creatinine concentration of 0.4 mg/dl , albumin concentration of 1.4 g/dl , and cholesterol concentration of 569 mg/dl. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no blood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Nephrotic syndrome due to focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis

correctExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of loss of normal size and charge filtration capability of the glomerular capillary and Bowman capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, and proteinuria. Complications include hypercoagulability caused by urinary loss of antithrombin-3 and infection caused by urinary loss y-globulins. The loss of proteins and decreased serum oncotic pressure in nephrotic syndrome leads to hepatic protein synthesis, especially of lipoproteins, which can contribute to hyperlipidemia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (Choice A) is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by dark colored urine, hypertension, hematuria, and proteinuria following an infection with group A streptococci. Minimal change disease is a nephrotic syndrome, characterized by massive proteinuria without hematuria. Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (Choice B) is typically associated with infection from enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7. It classically presents in children with bloody diarrhea accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Choice C) is a small-vessel vasculitis that occurs in children and typically presents with gravity-dependent purpura (eg, buttocks, legs, and feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain (eg, intussusception). Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Choice E) is a nephrotic syndrome that can result in proteinuria and pitting edema. However, FSGS is commonly associated with sickle cell disease, opioid abuse, and HIV infection, and is characterized by segmental sclerosis of the glomeruli. Educational Objectives: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, and proteinuria.

questionStem: A 2-year-old child with sickle cell hemoglobinopathy has a 2-week history of a paroxysmal cough followed by vomiting. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 32,000/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 10% Lymphocytes 85% Monocytes 5% An x-ray of the chest shows perihilar infiltrates. Which of the following vaccines could have prevented this condition? A Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular P.ertussis
correctExplanation: Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing are concerning for pertussis. Pertussis occurs because of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after one to two weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothorax. Often, such coughing fits are accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve during the convalescent stage, which lasts from one to four weeks. Pertussis toxin causes impaired recruitment and migration of phagocytes and production of inflammatory mediators. Patients often have significant lymphocytosis. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization in the form of acellular pertussis, typically administered along with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines. The Centers for Disease Control (CDC) recommends administering the vaccine in a multiple dose series beginning at two months of age. Pertussis is treated with antibiotics (typically macrolides) and supportive care.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Haemophi/us influenzae type b-protein conjugate (Choice B) vaccine uses capsular polysaccharide in conjugation with toxoid protein for prevention of infections caused by H. influenzae type b. H. influenzae is a Gram-negative bacterium that can result in various mucosal infections such as conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, and pneumonia. It was the leading cause of epiglottitis in children prior to widespread immunization. The CDC recommends administering H. influenzae type b-protein conjugate in a four-dose series beginning at age two months. Influenza virus (Choice C) vaccine prevents infection by influenza virus, an orthomyxovirus which is transmitted via respiratory droplets and causes seasonal pandemics. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgias, malaise, headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Pneumonia may develop. Influenza does not typically cause paroxysmal coughing. The CDC recommends annual influenza virus vaccination beginning at age greater than six months. Measles-mumps-rubella (Choice D) vaccine prevents measles, mumps, and rubella infection, which can cause different viral syndromes. None of these viruses cause paroxysmal coughing. The CDC recommends vaccination with measles-mumps-rubella in a two-dose series beginning at age one year. Pneumococcal (Choice E) vaccine prevents infections with Streptococcus pneumoniae, which can cause pneumonia and meningitis. It does not cause paroxysmal coughing. The CDC recommends vaccination with pneumococcal vaccine in a four-dose series beginning at age two months. Educational Objective: Pertussis occurs because of an infection from 8. pertussis and may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing that may be accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. Pertussis can be prevented by immunization with the diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis vaccine, which is given as a multiple dose series beginning at age two months.

questionStem: A 5-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of daily episodes of vomiting after feedings . Her mother reports that the episodes began shortly after birth and that the vomiting is occasionally bilious. Her diet consists of soy-based formula ; trials of multiple infant formulas have not stopped the vomiting . Abdominal examination shows no distention or tenderness . There are no masses. Normal bowel sounds are heard. An upper gastrointestinal series is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

This leaves the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. The cecum also remains in an abnormal position within the mid-upper abdomen instead of the right lower quadrant and is attached to the lateral abdominal wall by fibrous bands, which cross over the top of the duodenum and can also cause constriction. This leaves the small intestine at risk for volvulus originating at the base of the SMA. While most patients present in the first year of life, some individuals do not present until later childhood or adulthood. In this case, the patient's upper gastrointestinal barium series demonstrates the presence of the small intestine only within the right abdomen. In its usual anatomic position, the duodenum crosses the midline toward the ligament of Treitz and the remaining small intestine courses throughout the abdominal quadrants.
