A 5-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of daily episodes of vomiting after feedings . Her mother reports that the episodes began shortly after birth and that the vomiting is occasionally bilious. Her diet consists of soy-based formula ; trials of multiple infant formulas have not stopped the vomiting. Abdominal examination shows no distention or tenderness . There are no masses . Normal bowel sounds are heard . An upper gastrointestinal series is shown . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cyclic vomiting syndrome B) Gastroesophageal reflux disease C) Hiatal hernia D) Intestinal malrotation E) Pyloric stenosis CorrectAnswer: D. Intestinal malrotation is a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development. This leaves the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. The cecum also remains in an abnormal position within the mid-upper abdomen instead of the right lower quadrant and is attached to the lateral abdominal wall by fibrous bands, which cross over the top of the duodenum and can also cause constriction. This leaves the small intestine at risk for volvulus originating at the base of the SMA. While most patients present in the first year of life, some individuals do not present until later childhood or adulthood. In this case, the patient's upper gastrointestinal barium series demonstrates the presence of the small intestine only within the right abdomen. In its usual anatomic position, the duodenum crosses the midline toward the ligament of Treitz and the remaining small intestine courses throughout the abdominal quadrants. Thus, these imaging findings suggest malrotation of the small intestine. Mal rotation of the intestines predisposes to intestinal obstruction. In this case, the persistent vomiting of bilious emesis suggests a partial small bowel obstruction secondary to the patient's malrotation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cyclic vomiting syndrome (Choice A) is an idiopathic disorder seen in both children and adults characterized by recurrent episodes of vomiting with periods of normal health between episodes. In this case, the bilious nature of the vomit suggests that it is attributable to a structural cause instead. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) (Choice B) is caused by acid reflux into the lower esophagus. This commonly occurs as a result of increased intra-abdominal pressure or diminished closing pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter permitting acidic contents of the stomach to reflux into the esophagus. In an infant, gastroesophageal reflux disease presents with frequent regurgitation without excessive irritability. Bilious vomiting is a warning sign of a structural cause of vomiting rather than GERD. Hiatal hernia (Choice C) is caused by a defect in the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus that allows the lower esophageal sphincter and variable amounts of the stomach to be displaced into the thorax. It can cause heartburn, nausea or emesis, dysphagia, regurgitation, and shortness of breath. It does not cause bilious emesis or the radiographic findings seen in this case. Pyloric stenosis (Choice E) is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings, and begins around three to six weeks of age. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feeding, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Educational Objective: Intestinal malrotation is a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development, leaving the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the SMA, instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. It can be recognized on imaging by the presence of small intestine in the right abdomen only. Mal rotation increases the risk for volvulus of the small bowel at the base of the SMA (midgut volvulus), which causes small bowel obstruction.

questionStem: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of mild neck tenderness . She has not had fever, fatigue, sensitivity to hot or cold, or changes in weight. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . Her mother has systemic lupus erythematosus . The patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 112/72 mm Hg. Examination shows normal skin texture. There is no exophthalmos . The neck is supple; there is no lymphadenopathy . The thyroid gland is diffusely enlarged; no nodules are palpated. Serum studies show: Thyroid-stimulating hormone 3.9 µU/ml Thyroxine (T 4) 10 µg/dl Triiodothyronine (T :i) 135 ng/dl The patient's serum thyroid antiperoxidase antibody concentration is 1000 IU/ml (N<20). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is the most common form of thyroiditis and is characterized by the presence of antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies. Female patients are disproportionately affected compared to male patients. The early stages of Hashimoto thyroiditis can present with neck swelling and a diffusely enlarged, nontender thyroid gland. The patient may display evidence of hyperthyroidism from destruction of thyroid follicular cells and the unregulated release of thyroid hormone. During the chronic stages of Hashimoto thyroiditis, the patient typically develops primary hypothyroidism from the underlying inflammatory destruction of normal thyroid parenchyma and resultant insufficient production of thyroid hormone. Signs and symptoms during this stage include fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, myxedema, and dry, cool skin. Fine needle biopsy demonstrates lymphoid infiltrate with the presence of follicles and Hiirthle cells. Treatment is with oral replacement of thyroid hormone.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute suppurative thyroiditis (Choice A) presents with rapid onset of neck pain, tenderness, erythema, and warmth to touch , as well as symptoms of hyperthyroidism secondary to destruction of thyroid follicular cells. Commonly implicated organisms include Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species. Endemic goiter (Choice C) is caused by dietary iodine deficiency. It is rare in developed countries because of the routine fortification of common food staples, such as salt, with iodine. Graves disease (Choice D) is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in children and adolescents, as well as in adults, and it is caused by an autoantibody that activates thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptors on the thyroid. It presents with symptoms of hyperthyroidism, pretibial myxedema, and thyroid ophthalmopathy, which can cause diplopia, proptosis, and restrictive strabismus. Serum concentrations of TSH are typically reduced and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies would not be present. Thyroid carcinoma (Choice E) is typically non-functional and does not secrete thyroid hormone. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is encountered most frequently. Educational Objective: Chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is the most common form of thyroiditis and is characterized by the presence of antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies. Patients with chronic disease present with signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism, including fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, myxedema, and dry, cool skin. Patients in the acute stage of the disease may experience mild neck discomfort, although the thyroid is not usually tender.

questionStem: A 14-year-old boy with a cardiac murmur is brought to the physician for a school physical examination . He reports that during this past soccer season , he easily became short of breath at times but did not seek medical attention . He has no symptoms of chest pain, palpitations , or syncope , and he appears healthy. His pulse is 72/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 126/42 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a blowing diastolic murmur at the upper right sternal border; there is no systolic murmur. Radial and pedal pulses are 3+ bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Left ventricular volume overload as a result of aortic insufficiency (Al) explains this patient's widened pulse pressure, blowing diastolic murmur, and bounding radial pulses in addition to his exertional symptoms. The causes of Al, also called aortic regurgitation, include bicuspid aortic valve, aortic root dilation, and a history of rheumatic heart disease. It is also commonly associated with syndromes such as Marfan and Turner syndrome. Al results from an incompetent aortic valve that allows retrograde blood flow from the aortic root to the left ventricle (LV) during diastole. This results in an increased LV end-diastolic volume (EDV) as both blood from the aorta and the left atrium fill the LV. Increased volume stretches the compliant ventricle thereby increasing myocardial contractility, which is reflected as an increased stroke volume (SV) and a comparatively increased cardiac output. Over time, eccentric hypertrophy of the LV leads to loss of normal compliance and progressive LV systolic dysfunction.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) (Choice A) is not a feature of isolated Al. Increased PVR occurs in conditions such as pulmonary hypertension or pulmonic stenosis. Eventually, left-sided heart failure can lead to increased PVR, but this occurs over time and the patient in this case shows no symptoms of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale. Increased systemic cardiac output (Choice B) is incorrect. In compensated Al, the cardiac output is maintained, but over time the progressive hypertrophy of the LV in combination with ongoing aortic regurgitation leads to systolic dysfunction and decreased cardiac output. Increased systemic vascular resistance (SVR) (Choice C) is incorrect. SVR tends to be relatively normal in individuals with chronic compensated Al, although they tend to have a greater disparity between systolic and diastolic pressures. The large volume ejected during systole transiently increases the systolic pressure while the regurgitant volume back into the LV leads to a lower than expected diastolic pressure. Left ventricular pressure overload (Choice D) is incorrect. In young patients with chronic Al and no evidence of heart failure, the LV is able to compensate for increased end-diastolic volume by distending, thereby maintaining a normal LV end-diastolic pressure. Over time, however, eccentric hypertrophy can cause diastolic dysfunction and increased LV pressure. Educational Objective: Al results in an increased LV end-diastolic volume as regurgitant blood from the aorta enters the LV during diastole, which can be auscultated as a diastolic murmur. The retrograde flow of blood during diastole results in a lower diastolic pressure, which is reflected as an increased pulse pressure.

questionStem: A 15-month-old boy is brought to the physician for an initial examination . According to his mother and previous medical records , he has been healthy, and developmental milestones are appropriate for age. At his last examination 3 months ago, he was at the 25th percentile for length and weight. Today, he is at the 25th percentile for length and the 10th percentile for weight. Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of his poor weight gain?

choices.A: Recommend a diet diary with calorie counts
choices.C: Test the stool for reducing substances and fecal fat
choices.D: Admit to the hospital for observation
choices.E: Obtain an x-ray of the abdomen

correctExplanation: This child demonstrates a decreased velocity of weight gain compared to his growth in length, raising the concern for a diagnosis of poor weight gain and malnutrition. Poor weight gain is a common diagnosis seen in primary care offices in approximately 5% of pediatric patients. Risk factors include prematurity, developmental delay, congenital abnormalities, or any condition resulting in inadequate intake, absorption, or metabolism of nutrients. Poverty, social isolation, certain nutritional beliefs and practices, poor parenting skills, substance abuse, violence, or other abuse also predispose to poor weight gain. The first step in evaluation of poor weight gain is to take a thorough history of dietary practices and review of systems. If no suspected underlying organic cause is found, management of mild malnutrition should involve parental education and dietary advice, changes to dietary practices, provision of home-based support and referral to community or governmental programs to increase access to food. Recommending a diet diary with calorie counts will both investigate whether inadequate caloric intake is the cause of the child's poor weight gain and also assist caregivers in creating a personalized feeding plan.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reevaluating weight in 1 week (Choice B) without an associated intervention will not likely improve this patient's weight gain. After initiating a dietary plan, close follow up is warranted, but this alone is insufficient. Test the stool for reducing substances and fecal fat (Choice C) may be performed in children whose poor weight gain has not resolved with appropriate dietary intervention to investigate malabsorption as a potential cause. It is not warranted prior to attempting dietary intervention in an otherwise asymptomatic child. Admit to the hospital for observation (Choice D) is not necessary at this time as conservative measures including dietary changes have not yet been tried. There is no reason to suspect that this weight loss is caused by caregiver neglect or non-accidental trauma, in which case admission would be appropriate. Obtain an x-ray of the abdomen (Choice E) is not necessary in this case as the patient has no symptoms, such as vomiting, abdominal pain, decreased appetite, or diarrhea, suggestive of an abdominal pathology. Educational Objective: A decreased velocity of weight gain compared to growth in length raises the concern for poor weight gain and malnutrition. A diet diary with calorie counts will investigate whether inadequate caloric intake is the cause of the child's poor weight gain.

questionStem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of swelling of the eyelids and feet for 3 days . Over the past week , she has had decreased urinary frequency . Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat that resolved spontaneously . Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1 °F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg. Examination shows periorbital , pretibial , and pedal edema . Urinalysis shows : Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypertension?
correctExplanation: pH Specific gravity Blood Protein RBC WBC RBC casts 6 1.015 large 3+ too numerous to count 5-10/hpf 10-20/hpf Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by dark colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, hematuria, and proteinuria following an infection with group A streptococcus. Glomerular injury in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis involves immune complex formation in the glomerulus, and light microscopy shows deposits of C3 and lgG in the glomerulus and mesangium. Urinalysis shows hematuria and variable proteinuria, with or without red blood cell casts. Hypertension associated with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by salt and fluid retention resulting in volume overload. Fluid retention can lead to generalized edema including periorbital, pretibial, and pedal edema. It can also lead to complications involving heart failure, pulmonary edema, and respiratory distress.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Catecholamine excess (Choice A) can occur in pheochromocytoma, which presents with episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, agitation, tachycardia, tachypnea, and treatment-refractory hypertension. It is the most common primary tumor of the adrenal medulla, and is marked by the functional secretion of epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, which cause episodic hyperadrenergic symptoms. Idiopathic hypertension (Choice B) would be the diagnosis if there was no preceding cause of hypertension, but this patient presents with a nephritic syndrome caused by poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis as a cause of hypertension. Mineralocorticoid excess (Choice C) can occur in hyperaldosteronism and increased secretion of aldosterone from the adrenal gland. This can be seen with an adrenal adenoma or adrenal hyperplasia and presents with hypertension, normal or decreased potassium concentrations, and metabolic alkalosis. It would not present with hematuria and proteinuria. Stimulation of the parasympathetic system (Choice D) can occur with cholinergic toxicity and would lead to excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, altered mental status, and miosis. It would be unlikely to cause hypertension. Increased sympathetic, not parasympathetic, system activation can lead to hypertension. Educational Objective: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by dark colored urine, hypertension, hematuria, and proteinuria following an infection with group A streptococcus. Hypertension associated with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by salt and fluid retention.

questionStem: A 3-day-old girl with Down syndrome has not had a bowel movement since birth. She feeds poorly but has not vomited . She has not had any other symptoms . She was born at term to a 39-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. Rupture of the membranes occurred 6 hours prior to delivery ; there was no meconium staining of fluid. Apgar scores were 6 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . The patient's temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 40/min , and blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg. Examination shows epicanthal folds , white stellate spots on the irides, single palmar creases , and wide spaces between the great and second toes. The abdomen is soft and nontender ; there is no organomegaly . Muscle tone is decreased in the trunk . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's failure to pass stool?

choices.A: Absence of ganglion cells in the bowel wall
choices.B: Dilation of lymphatic vessels of the bowel

correctExplanation: Congenital megacolon (also known as Hirschsprung disease or intestinal aganglionosis) is caused by the congenital absence of the distal portion of the myenteric plexus, a part of the enteric nervous system located between the inner and outer layers of the muscularis externa in the bowel wall. During development, this plexus migrates cephalad to caudal and incomplete migration results in absence of the plexus in the distal portion of the gastrointestinal tract. This often leads to an inability to pass meconium within the first few days of life and, eventually, large bowel obstruction. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a common clinical finding. Barium enema is used to evaluate for congenital megacolon in children. Congenital megacolon is associated with Down syndrome. Patients with Down syndrome are also at increased risk for dementia (Alzheimer type), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia, cardiac septal defects, and duodenal atresia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dilation of lymphatic vessels of the bowel (Choice B) caused by obstruction is found in intestinal lymphangiectasia. Loss of lymphocytes into the gut secondary to this dilation can lead to lymphopenia and subsequent immunosuppression. It does not contribute to failure to pass meconium after birth. Duodenal atresia (Choice C) is caused by failure of re-canalization of duodenal lumen. Duodenal atresia presents with vomiting and abdominal distension, as well as distension of the stomach and duodenum on abdominal x-ray. Like congenital megacolon, duodenal atresia is more common in children with Down syndrome. Pancreatic enzyme insufficiency (Choice D) is seen in cystic fibrosis because of destruction of the pancreatic duct. The absence of the digestive enzymes made by the pancreas leads to malnutrition (eg, cachexia, muscle wasting), weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, and frequent, loose, foul-smelling, sometimes oily stools (steatorrhea). Cystic fibrosis may also present with meconium ileus, another cause of failure to pass stool after birth. However, this patient's presentation is more characteristic of congenital megacolon. Villous atrophy (Choice E) in the small bowel is a characteristic finding of Celiac disease. Celiac disease is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy which causes inflammatory infiltration of the proximal small bowel, which leads to characteristic intraepithelial lymphocytosis, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia. Malabsorption of substances in the proximal small bowel ensues, which presents symptomatically as chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies. Educational Objective: Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) is caused by the congenital absence of the distal portion of the myenteric plexus, which causes failure to pass meconium and constipation. It is associated with Down syndrome. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a common clinical finding, and a barium enema is used to evaluate for the condition.

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing lethargy and jaundice over the past week . At birth, he had jaundice treated with phototherapy for 5 days . His father had a splenectomy at the age of 6 years . Developmental milestones and diet are normal for age. Examination shows mild scleral icterus . A grade 2/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard . The spleen tip is palpated 4 cm below the left costal margin . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Lymphocytes Monocytes Reticulocyte count Serum total bilirubin 8.3 g/dL 6500/mm 3 40% 55% 5% 10% 5 mg/dL Direct and indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) tests are negative . A blood smear is most likely to show which of the following types of erythrocytes?
correctExplanation: Normocytic and normochromic is the correct answer. This patient with evidence of hemolytic anemia, increased reticulocyte count, and a family history of similar symptoms requiring splenectomy likely has hereditary spherocytosis (HS). HS can occur if there are mutations in one or more proteins that link the erythrocyte inner membrane skeleton to the outer lipid bilayer, and include mutations in spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, and band 4.2. These mutations are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Spherocytosis results from progressive loss of the erythrocyte membrane over time and gives the erythrocytes a spherical shape; the surface area decreases but the volume of the cell remains unchanged. This impairs the erythrocyte's ability to confirm in small vessels of the microcirculation, especially within the spleen , where spherocytes accumulate. Patients often present with splenomegaly, hemolytic anemia, and pigmented gallstones. Peripheral smear will show normocytic, normochromic erythrocytes and, if there is a high degree of hemolysis, reticulocytes, which appear as larger, pale blue erythrocytes. Definitive management involves splenectomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Macrocytic and hyperchromic (Choice A) erythrocytes are seen in vitamin B 12 or folate deficiency, which may occur in pediatric patients with malabsorptive conditions such as celiac disease. In older patients and adults, it can be seen in gastric bypass, chronic alcohol use, and pernicious anemia. Macrocytic and hypochromic (Choice B) erythrocytes may result from a combination of diseases such as vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency (macrocytosis), iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, or thalassemia (hypochromia). Microcytic and hypochromic (Choice C) erythrocytes are seen in iron deficiency, which can result from chronic blood loss. It would be uncommon in such a young patient without evidence of chronic gastrointestinal bleeding. Normocytic and hypochromic (Choice D) erythrocytes are commonly seen in thalassemia. Additional findings of peripheral smear include target cells. Educational Objective: Autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins cause hereditary spherocytosis through loss of the normal connection between the inner membrane skeleton and the outer lipid bilayer. Clinical symptoms include jaundice, splenomegaly, and anemia. Peripheral smear shows normocytic, normochromic anemia with the presence of spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy.

questionStem: A 1-day-old newborn is jittery and irritable . He was born at term to a 25-year-old primigravid woman who received irregular prenatal care; maternal serology screening on admission was negative for hepatitis B, rubella , HIV, and syphilis . The newborn weighs 4706 g (10 lb 6 oz) and is pink. The anterior fontanelle is 1.5 cm, and the posterior fontanelle is barely patent. The lungs are clear to auscultation . Cardiac examination shows a regular rate and rhythm with a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur throughout the precordium and strong femoral pulses bilaterally. The abdomen is soft without masses or hepatosplenomegaly . Genital examination shows no abnormalities . Neurologic examination shows slight jitteriness but normal tone . Which of the following is the most likely cause of the newborn's neurologic findings?
correctExplanation: Excessive fetal exposure to insulin in utero can cause macrosomia, neonatal respiratory distress syndrome or hyaline membrane disease, and hypoglycemia in the newborn. Human placental lactogen produced by the placenta increases maternal insulin resistance. This leads to increased concentrations of glucose in the maternal circulation, and subsequently, the fetal circulation. Fetal hyperglycemia in turn causes the fetus to produce excess insulin and decrease the rate of gluconeogenesis. The insulin then acts as a growth factor, leading to macrosomia (as in this patient), and it inhibits the production of surfactant, which can lead to respiratory distress syndrome. After birth, the newborn continues to synthesize insulin but is no longer exposed to maternal blood glucose which leads to hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia presents in the newborn with tremors, diaphoresis, irritability, lethargy, and seizures. Treatment is supportive and includes administration of supplemental glucose while neonatal endocrine regulation self-corrects. Maternal diabetes mellitus, which is usually diagnosed by a routine glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks' gestation, can also cause other neonatal complications including congenital cardiac and neurologic abnormalities (eg, patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, caudal regression), preterm delivery, polycythemia, and hyperbilirubinemia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A) causes decreased serum cortisol and presents with fatigue, hypotension, hypoglycemia, and abdominal pain. In children, it is commonly caused by congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which leads to varying concentrations of mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and androgens depending on the enzyme affected. In general, it presents with ambiguous genitalia or precocious puberty and can present with salt wasting in infancy. This patient has a normal genital examination, making this less likely. Hypermagnesemia (Choice B) in infants can be caused by magnesium sulfate administration in the mother in preeclampsia or eclampsia. It causes hypotonia and respiratory depression in the newborn but does not cause jitteriness. Hypocalcemia (Choice C) presents with jitteriness, myoclonus, and seizures, as well as occasional laryngospasm or bronchospasm. It is commonly associated with DiGeorge syndrome, which causes parathyroid hypoplasia, and resultant severe hypocalcemia. However, DiGeorge syndrome is associated with craniofacial abnormalities that this patient does not exhibit. Hypothyroidism (Choice E) presents in the first few months of life with feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedema, macroglossia, large fontanelles, hypotonia, and hypothermia. It is not generally apparent at birth. Educational Objective: Maternal diabetes mellitus exposes a fetus to increased concentrations of blood glucose, in response to which the fetus increases production of insulin and decreases gluconeogenesis. Following birth, this can lead to postnatal hypoglycemia as the newborn is no longer exposed to increased concentrations of blood glucose in the maternal circulation. This presents with tremors, diaphoresis, irritability, lethargy, and seizures.

questionStem: Twelve hours after undergoing circumcision , a 3-day-old boy has persistent bleeding at his circumcision site. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation to a 23-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He was given an intramuscular injection of vitamin K immediately after delivery. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 55/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Examination shows a prominent right parietal cephalohematoma . There is an ecchymosis at the vitamin K injection site and continuous oozing of blood at the circumcision site. Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings? A Factor VIII deficiency
correctExplanation: Hematocrit 53% Leukocyte count 10,500/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 50% Basophils 4% Lymphocytes 40% Monocytes 6% Platelet count 350,000/mm 3 Prothrombin time 12 sec {INR=1.05) Partial thromboplastin time 90 sec Factor VIII deficiency resulting in hemophilia A is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with uncontrolled bleeding from his circumcision site, large right cephalohematoma, an abnormally prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT), normal prothrombin time (PT), and normal platelet count. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive condition and is therefore more commonly seen in males, while most females are silent carriers. It is caused by an absence or deficiency of factor VIII, which is a component of the intrinsic clotting cascade. Factor VIII is required as a cofactor for the activation of factor X to factor Xa, which in turn converts prothrombin to thrombin to complete the process of clot formation. The PTT measures the activity of the intrinsic pathway and will be prolonged in cases of hemophilia A, while the PT measures the activity of factor VII (extrinsic pathway), which is normal in patients with this disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Platelet dysfunction {Choice B) can be inherited or acquired and can also result in prolonged bleeding, but the PTT is usually normal, while bleeding time would be increased. Examples of inherited platelet disorders include Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and platelet granule disorders. Sepsis {Choice C) is an unlikely diagnosis in this patient without fever or signs of infection. Common infections that cause sepsis in the newborn period include meningitis and pneumonia. Vitamin K deficiency {Choice D) is unlikely because this child was given a dose of vitamin K, which is adequate to correct any deficiency. Additionally, this would present with a prolonged PT. von Willebrand factor deficiency {Choice E) can present with bleeding and is caused by quantitative or qualitative abnormality of von Willebrand factor (vWF), which binds platelets and subendothelial collagen in primary hemostasis. Impaired platelet adherence leads to prolonged bleeding time. It can present with epistaxis, gingival bleeding, petechiae, easy bruising, and menorrhagia. Educational Objective: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disease resulting in deficiency or absence of factor VIII. It presents with prolonged bleeding following tissue injury. Laboratory studies will show a prolonged PTT but normal PT and normal platelet count. Treatment is with recombinant factor VIII.

questionStem: Four hours after an elective cesarean delivery at 38 weeks' gestation , a newborn has nasal flaring and tachypnea . There was no meconium staining of the amniotic fluid. The mother received regular prenatal care, and she had no fever or illness during pregnancy . The newborn's temperature is 37.6°C (99.?°F), pulse is 180/min, and respirations are 80/min . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. The lungs are clear to auscultation . An x-ray of the chest shows prominent pulmonary vascular markings , fluid lines in the fissures , and a flat diaphragm . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.F: Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn

correctExplanation: Transient tachypnea of the newborn presents within a few hours of birth with tachypnea (respirations greater than 60/min), and signs of respiratory distress, such as cyanosis, nasal flaring, and intercostal or subcostal retractions. It is caused by a delay in the resorption of fetal amniotic fluid in the alveoli. The residual fluid in the lung decreases the pulmonary compliance, which leads to an increased work of breathing, tachypnea, and hypoxia in the newborn, and to air trapping through relative compression the bronchioles. Auscultation of the chest is typically normal. Chest x-ray will show a flattened diaphragm and pulmonary congestion with fluid in the interlobular fissures, as well as occasional pleural effusions. Risk factors for its development include preterm birth, diabetes in the mother, cesarean delivery, and maternal asthma. Treatment is typically supportive with supplemental oxygen as needed, with the majority of cases resolving in 24 to 48 hours.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Aspiration pneumonia (Choice A) occurs because of the inhalation of orogastric contents into the airway, and most commonly occurs due to dysfunction of the swallowing mechanisms or an inability to protect the airway. Meconium aspiration can occur in the newborn, which can lead to airway obstruction, inflammation, and infection. However, this patient's amniotic fluid was clear, making meconium aspiration unlikely. Bacterial pneumonia (Choice B) in the newborn can be caused by infected amniotic fluid, maternal infection, or aspiration of meconium. It commonly presents with fever or hypothermia, respiratory distress, tachycardia, and a chest x-ray with an area of consolidation. This patient is afebrile, and his chest x-ray shows pulmonary edema, rather than a new infiltrate. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (Choice C) is a chronic lung disease that occurs in preterm infants, often requiring prolonged oxygen supplementation. It is caused by alveolar hypoplasia with increased wall thickening, as well as abnormalities of pulmonary vasculature that lead to increased pulmonary resistance. This patient was born at term, making this unlikely. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Choice D) typically presents in older patients with exertional dyspnea and a chronic cough. Physical examination may disclose inspiratory crackles, and chest imaging will show honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. It would be unlikely to present in a newborn. Pulmonary hemorrhage (Choice E) typically presents with dyspnea, hypoxia, tachycardia, and profound hemoptysis, which may be life-threatening. In children, it can occur with foreign body aspiration, trauma, and bronchiectasis, as well as rheumatologic and hematologic disorders. This patient has no reported history of hemoptysis. Respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn (Choice F) occurs in preterm infants because of surfactant deficiency that leads to alveolar collapse. This leads to increased work of breathing, hypoxemia, and cyanosis. It is typically apparent at birth and can be differentiated from transient tachypnea of the newborn with a chest x-ray that shows bilateral ground glass opacities with air bronchograms. Educational Objective: Transient tachypnea of the newborn presents with tachypnea, respiratory distress, cyanosis, and hypoxia caused by a delay in the resorption of amniotic fluid in the alveoli. The fluid leads to decreased compliance and air trapping. Risk factors include preterm delivery, maternal diabetes or asthma, and cesarean delivery. Chest x-ray will show a flattened diaphragm and pulmonary vascular congestion with fluid in the interlobular fissures.

questionStem: A 3714-g (8-lb 3-oz) newborn is delivered at 43 weeks' gestation to a 32-year-old woman , gravida 4, para 3. Apgar scores are 3 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . The newborn's skin and nails are meconium stained, and he is cyanotic. He is immediately intubated and mechanically ventilated at an F102 of 100%. No meconium is noted below the vocal cords prior to insertion of the endotracheal tube. One hour later, he remains cyanotic . The lungs are clear to auscultation . Umbilical arterial blood gas analysis shows : pH 7.1 Pco2 34 mm Hg Po2 26 mm Hg An x-ray of the chest shows no cardiomegaly or pulmonary infiltrates . Echocardiography shows normal cardiac anatomy with a right-to-left shunt across the foramen ovale. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
correctExplanation: Failure of pulmonary vasodilation resulting in significant pulmonary hypertension is the most likely cause of this patient's right-to-left shunt across the foramen ovale and persistent hypoxemia. Normal fetal circulation is unique in that oxygenated blood arrives from the maternal circulation via the umbilical vein and reaches the inferior vena cava directly. From there, oxygenated blood is shunted from the right atrium to the left atrium, to the left ventricle (LV), and then to the systemic circulation. Oxygenated blood that reaches the right ventricle (RV) and the pulmonary arteries is shunted through the ductus arteriosus (DA) to the aortic arch. Before birth the fetal lungs are filled with amniotic fluid and the pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high. Under normal circumstances, the first breath leads to a decrease in PVR as pulmonary vessels dilate. Peripartum asphyxia, as in this case, in addition to acidosis, impairs the normal transition from an increased to decreased PVR state. Despite adequate delivery of oxygen after intubation, a persistently increased PVR impairs oxygenation. As such, pulmonary hypertension most likely explains this patient's persistent hypoxemia. Meconium aspiration also causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch, but it is the result of an obstructed bronchial tree with normal perfusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Closure of the ductus arteriosus (Choice A), which is a shunt between the pulmonary arteries and the aortic arch, typically occurs within several days after birth. Failure to close results in an extracardiac left-to-right shunt and classically presents with a continuous machine-like murmur. Closure of foramen ovale (Choice B) occurs within the first 6 months of life and is a normal occurrence. Persistence is known as a patent foramen ovale and causes left-to-right shunting. If large enough, this can eventually result in right-sided hypertrophy and heart failure with shunt reversal. Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance (Choice C) is incorrect, as this is a normal occurrence after birth. The decrease in PVR improves oxygenation. Increased peripheral vascular resistance (Choice E) causes systemic hypertension but would not affect oxygenation as it has no effect on ventilation or perfusion of the lungs. lntracardiac left-to-right shunt (Choice F) can occur as a result of a patent foramen ovale or a ventricular septal defect, which allows oxygenated blood to re-enter the pulmonary vasculature. This would not result in hypoxemia. Educational Objective: PVR normally decreases immediately after birth to allow for deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to enter the pulmonary vasculature where it is oxygenated. In instances of perinatal asphyxia, the normal decrease in PVR is disrupted leading to persistently increased PVR, otherwise known as pulmonary hypertension. This restricts the blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature and can cause persistent hypoxemia despite adequate oxygen delivery and ventilation.

questionStem: A previously healthy 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of a 4-month history of episodes of bright red blood in her stool. The episodes are not associated with pain, constipation , or diarrhea . Growth and development are appropriate for age . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min , respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg. Examination of the face shows areas of hyperpigmentation on the lips and buccal mucosa . A photograph of the mouth is shown . Examination of the anus shows no fissures or signs of trauma . Digital rectal examination shows bright red blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a genetic condition inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is characterized by the triad of colonic polyps, mucocutaneous hyperpigmented macules, and an increased risk for gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal malignancy. In this syndrome, hamartomatous polyps are scattered throughout the gastrointestinal tract and are associated with an increased risk for colorectal and gastric carcinoma. Acute bleeding episodes from one of these polyps leading to bright red blood in the stool, as in this case, are common, but bleeding may also be occult and cause an iron deficiency anemia before it is recognized. Yearly complete blood count to screen for anemia is recommended. Baseline endoscopic evaluation utilizing both upper endoscopy and colonoscopy is recommended to evaluate for malignancy. Blue­ gray pigmented macules are scattered primarily in the perioral region and on the lips. They may be confused for freckles but are caused by increased numbers of dermal macrophages containing melanin rather than increased size of melanosomes. The blue-gray cutaneous macules in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are not malignant.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Stool culture (Choice A) is an appropriate next step in the work up of bloody diarrhea thought to be caused by a bacterial infection such as Escherichia coli or Shigel/a. However, this patient has had blood in her ........ ~ ........................ .

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by friends after she passed out at a party. She has a history of substance abuse , and they say that she drank more than eight glasses of alcohol during the past 2 hours. On arrival , she does not respond to painful stimuli. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 61/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows scleral icterus . The liver edge is palpated 1 cm below the right costal margin . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management ?

choices.A: Determine the exact amount and type of alcohol ingested

correctExplanation: The patient presents after drinking a large amount of alcohol with altered mental status, obtundation, respiratory distress, and hypoxia. The patient also has signs of chronic excessive alcohol abuse including an enlarged liver palpated below the costal margin and scleral icterus, consistent with alcoholic hepatitis. The patient's obtunded mental status is also associated with disordered breathing, tachypnea, respiratory distress, and hypoxia. The initial management of this patient should include airway protection, including endotracheal intubation to support the patient's ventilation and oxygenation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Determining the exact amount and type of alcohol ingested {Choice A) and measurement of blood alcohol concentration {Choice B) may be helpful in the care of this patient, but would not be necessary in the emergency management of the patient with disordered breathing and oxygenation. Further elucidating the amount of alcohol ingested may be helpful to determine the time it may take for the patient to metabolize the alcohol. Nebulized acetylcysteine therapy {Choice C) is a mucolytic agent that has been used in the treatment of asthma, emphysema, bronchitis, cystic fibrosis, and diseases that may be complicated by mucous plugging of airways. It would not be indicated in this patient, as the patient's respiratory distress and hypoxia is more likely caused by alcohol intoxication. Hemodialysis {Choice E) is typically not used in the treatment of alcohol intoxication as the liver is usually able to metabolize alcohol. Dialysis may be helpful in patients with ethylene glycol poisoning and metabolic acidosis. Educational Objective: The initial management of an obtunded patient showing signs of respiratory distress should include airway protection, including endotracheal intubation to support the patient's ventilation and oxygenation.

questionStem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of a facial rash and fatigue . She has a 9-day history of stiffness and swelling of her fingers on awakening in the morning . She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . She appears tired and has mild chest pain with deep inspirations . Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 94/min and regular, respirations are 24/min , and blood pressure is 112/76 mm Hg. Examination shows a bright red rash over the cheeks and nose. Diffuse 1- to 2-cm lymph nodes are palpated in the anterior and posterior cervical chains . There are three nontender ulcers on the soft palate. The lungs are clear to auscultation . Heart sounds are normal. Examination of the extremities shows mild erythema , tenderness , and swelling of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints , knees, and metatarsophalangeal joints . Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and 1 + blood. Which of the following is most appropriate in determining appropriate management for this patient?
correctExplanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disorder with a wide range of presentations. In order to make a diagnosis of SLE, four of eleven criteria must be present. These include malar rash, photosensitivity, discoid rash, painless oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis (including pleuritis or pericarditis), neurologic disorder (seizures or psychosis), renal impairment, hematologic abnormalities (hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia, or thrombocytopenia), an abnormal antinuclear antibody assay, or lupus-specific autoantibodies (anti-DNA, anti-Smith, antiphospholipid antibody). The patient described has numerous of these criteria suggesting a diagnosis of SLE. Lupus nephritis is a complication of SLE and is common in younger female patients; it presents with hematuria and rising creatinine in SLE. Evaluation of lupus nephritis requires renal biopsy in order to accurately determine the type and extent of renal involvement. This information is vital for optimizing treatment of nephritis. For example, immunosuppressive therapy is warranted for active diffuse or focal proliferative lupus nephritis but not mild mesangial or mesangial proliferative lupus nephritis.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. X-rays of the knees (Choice A) is a commonly used modality to begin evaluation of knee pain. However, this patient has numerous other symptoms suggestive of a diagnosis of SLE. The arthritis of SLE is non-erosive and non-deforming. It is typically treated with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antimalarials, or glucocorticoids. Because of this, not only will x-rays of the knee likely be normal, but they will not change the management of this patient's arthritis. Her proteinuria and hematuria are much more concerning and an indication for renal biopsy. Echocardiography (Choice B) is used in evaluating pleural and pericardia! effusions. This patient does have pleuritic chest pain suggestive of pleuritis, but she is hemodynamically stable and has no abnormalities on her cardiac examination. The more pressing complication of SLE in this case, which requires further diagnostic effort, is lupus nephritis. MRI of the brain (Choice C) and cerebral angiography (Choice D) are both imaging modalities that may be used to evaluate a patient with neuropsychiatric symptoms caused by SLE. There is no evidence that this patient has neuropsychiatric symptoms, and thus, this imaging is not currently warranted. Educational Objective: SLE is an autoimmune connective tissue disease, one manifestation of which is lupus nephritis. Hematuria and proteinuria with a rising creatinine are characteristic of lupus nephritis. Renal biopsy is necessary to accurately determine the type and extent of renal involvement to optimize treatment.

questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of cough and nasal congestion . Her parents say that she has been tired and irritable for 6 months ; during this period , she has been sleeping excessively during the day and snoring loudly. Her pulse is 126/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 120/86 mm Hg. On examination , she has nasal congestion and breathes predominantly through her mouth . A grade 1/6 holosystolic murmur is heard in the fourth left parasternal space . There is tonsillar and adenoidal hypertrophy . An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly . Echocardiography shows right ventricular hypertrophy , pulmonary hypertension , and mild tricuspid regurgitation . Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?
correctExplanation: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common in the pediatric population and is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and snoring. Risk factors for pediatric OSA include adenotonsillar hypertrophy and obesity. Both lead to a decreased airway size and increased risk for airway obstruction during sleep, which in turn, leads to pulmonary hypertension. In this case, the x-ray and echocardiography findings indicate the presence of cor pulmonale, or right ventricular dysfunction caused by a primary disorder of the pulmonary system. Other complications of untreated OSA include systemic hypertension, left ventricular dysfunction, failure to thrive, and behavioral problems. This patient also demonstrates adenoid and tonsillar hypertrophy on examination. In children with this finding, the first-line treatment of OSA is adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy. In some cases, watchful waiting is appropriate, but only if the OSA is mild and there are no signs of complication. As this patient shows significant cardiovascular complications secondary to OSA, surgical removal of the adenoids and tonsils is necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Digoxin and diuretic therapy (Choice A) is a therapy used in management of congestive heart failure to improve the contractility of the heart and prevent volume overload. While these modalities may be needed as temporizing measures, they are not a long-term solution. Pulmonary vasodilator therapy (Choice B) is used in primary pulmonary hypertension to decrease the pressure within the pulmonary vasculature. This patient's pulmonary hypertension stems from her OSA. Dilating the pulmonary vasculature will not solve the underlying cause of the hypertension. Pulmonary artery banding (Choice C) is a therapy used in patients with left transposition of the great arteries to train the left ventricle to pump against the systemic circulation after surgical repair of the great arteries is completed. This patient does not require training of the left ventricle but rather decreased pulmonary resistance by treatment of OSA. Repair of tricuspid regurgitation (Choice E) is not appropriate in this patient as it does not address the cause underlying the valvular defect. This patient's tricuspid regurgitation is caused by the dilation of the right ventricle and widening of the valvular opening with inadequate coverage by the valve leaflets. After addressing the underlying cause of cardiomegaly, if the tricuspid regurgitation does not improve, surgical repair may be indicated, but it is not currently. Educational Objective: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and snoring. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is a common cause of OSA in children. If present, the first-line treatment of OSA is adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy.

questionStem: A previously healthy 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a rash over the eyelids and fingers for 1 week . Examination shows a violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids and an erythematous , atrophic , scaly lesion over the knuckles and dorsal surfaces of the finger joints . There is weakness of the proximal extremities and trunk. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune connective tissue disease affecting the skin and the proximal muscles. Cutaneous manifestations include pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope sign), light pink to lilac colored patches with telangiectasias on the upper back and sun-exposed chest, and dilated capillaries with drop out on the proximal nail folds. Juvenile dermatomyositis also commonly demonstrates calcinosis cutis, the deposition of calcium in the skin. An inflammatory infiltrate of the muscle occurs causing damage to the myocytes, leading to release of creatine kinase, an intracellular molecule. This can be used to monitor disease progress in dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis is also characterized by several autoantibodies. It demonstrates a positive antinuclear antibody and anti-Jo-1. Anti-SRP and anti-Mi-2 antibodies are also commonly seen. Dermatomyositis is less likely to be associated with malignancy in children than it is in adults. Treatment of dermatomyositis involves systemic steroids followed by long-term immunosuppressive therapy with medications such as methotrexate or azathioprine.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Eosinophilic granuloma (Choice B) is a form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis which primarily involves the bones. In children, these lytic bone lesions are commonly seen in the skull. Muscle weakness is not present. Inflammatory bowel disease (Choice C) comprises both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Both present with bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. Muscle weakness is not seen. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Choice D), or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, is characterized by fever, arthritis, an evanescent, pink-colored rash, and lymphadenopathy. Mixed connective tissue disease (Choice E) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease with overlapping, non-specific features of autoimmune connective tissue diseases including systemic lupus erythematosus, dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. This patient's symptoms are specific to dermatomyositis. Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) (Choice F) is a multisystemic inflammatory disease in children characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and erythema affecting the mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. Periarteritis nodosa (Choice G), now known as polyarteritis nodosa, is a medium-vessel vasculitis in which the muscular wall of a medium size artery becomes inflamed. Characteristic symptoms include fatigue, weight loss, weakness, fever, arthralgias, and skin ulcers. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (Choice H) is an autoimmune disease resulting in a constellation of symptoms including fever, rash, photosensitivity, renal disease, and nonerosive arthritis. The rash in SLE is seen over the malar prominences of the cheeks and spares the nasolabial folds. Eyelid involvement is not typical. Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) (Choice I) presents with taut, hardened skin, Raynaud phenomenon, renal failure, telangiectasias, cardiac fibrosis, esophageal dysmotility, and lower gastrointestinal tract fibrosis.

questionStem: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of rash and a 1-week history of low-grade fever and a mild headache . The rash began as a small red bump on the right thigh and now measures 12 cm. His temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6°F). Examination shows no other abnormalities except for the rash shown . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.C: Folliculitis I) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease)

correctExplanation: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, endemic in the Northeastern United States. In its early stages, it causes erythema chronicum migrans, which is an expanding rash with a central ring-like clearing as shown in this case. It can also be associated with a flu-like illness. In the early stages of Lyme disease, it can be treated with doxycycline, which acts by preventing the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosomes. Adverse effects of tetracycline antibiotics include gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, and in children, discoloration of teeth and inhibition of bone growth, which makes it contraindicated in pregnancy. Later stages of Lyme disease can be characterized by carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy {which is often bilateral), migratory arthralgias, and if left untreated, encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. Later stages of Lyme disease that affect the heart or central nervous system are generally treated with parenteral ceftriaxone.
incorrectExplanation: nd L. Atopic dermatitis {Choice A), or eczema, is characterized by pruritus, flexural eczema, a history of asthma or hay fever, and dry skin. The rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting and, with chronic scratching, becomes dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. Cellulitis {Choice B), folliculitis {Choice C), and impetigo {Choice F) are all superficial bacterial infections of the skin. Cellulitis presents with a warm, erythematous patch or plaque, folliculitis with follicle-centric pustules on hair-bearing areas, and impetigo with honey-colored crust typically around the mouth or nose in a child. An expanding, targetoid, erythematous patch is not characteristic of these infections. Herpes simplex {Choice D) virus typically begins with the formation of vesicles, which lyse and progress to shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous border. It is often accompanied by fever, chills, and lymphadenopathy. Herpes zoster {Choice E) commonly presents as a unilateral, dermatomal erythematous patch with overlying clear to yellow, grouped vesicles. It is caused by varicella-zoster virus, also known as human herpesvirus-3, which is transmitted via respiratory secretions and direct contact with infected skin lesions. It can be associated with neuropathic pain which can both precede and outlast the rash, but this is more common in the elderly than pediatric patients. Juvenile melanoma {Choice G) is suggested by a single lesion with asymmetry, irregular appearing borders, variable coloration, a diameter greater than 6 mm, and rapid evolution in characteristics. Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) {Choice I) is a multisystemic inflammatory disease in children characterized by fever for at least five days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and erythema affecting the mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. Neurofibromatosis {Choice J) is a genetically inherited disorder characterized by a constellation of cutaneous manifestations including neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, cafe-au-lait I d ·11 f kl" f h. h t . th· t" t . . .

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain, nausea , and vomiting that began 4 hours after attending a friend's birthday party. Cake and other pastries were served at the party. She appears acutely ill and mildly dehydrated . Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities of the skin. Bowel sounds are hyperactive . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive organism that is a common cause of cutaneous infections including impetigo, cellulitis, folliculitis, and furunculosis. Staphylococci, especially S. aureus, is associated with the secretion of several exotoxins, including enterotoxin, exfoliatoxin, and toxic shock syndrome toxin. Its enterotoxins commonly cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and intestinal cramping after ingestion of food contaminated by S. aureus. S. aureus enterotoxin is heat-stable and associated with the consumption of foods that are contaminated, often cream-based foods. Foods that are left at room temperature allow S. aureus to multiply and produce more enterotoxin. Ingestion of S. aureus enterotoxin leads to nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping that typically occurs within 6 hours.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Campylobacter jejuni (Choice A), enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (Choice C), nontyphoidal Salmonella species such as Salmonella enteritidis (Choice D), and Shigella sonnei (Choice E) classically present with mucosal inflammation and invasion, leading to a toxic appearance and bloody diarrhea. This patient is presenting with vomiting and abdominal cramping, not bloody diarrhea, making these organisms less likely. Clostridium botulinum (Choice B) creates a botulinum toxin which, if ingested, can also cause a foodborne gastroenteritis resulting in nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping; it may also result in neurologic symptoms and flaccid paralysis. However, symptoms typically begin between 18 to 36 hours after the toxin is ingested, later than those of S. aureus-induced foodborne illness. Educational Objective: Enterotoxins commonly cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and intestinal cramping within 6 hours after the ingestion of food contaminated by S. aureus.

questionStem: A 1-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-day history of decreased oral intake. Her mother says that the child has also had blood in her saliva. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Examination shows inflammation and erythema of the oral cavity with diffuse white plaques that bleed when scraped . There is a papular erythematous rash with satellite lesions over the diaper area. Which of the following is the most likely immune mechanism for these findings?
correctExplanation: Decreased T-lymphocyte activity is the most likely cause of this patient's white, bleeding oral lesions and papular erythematous rash in the diaper area with satellite lesions, which are both consistent with Candida albicans infection. There are many species of Candida, including C. albicans, C. glabrata, C. krusei, C. tropica/is, C. parapsilosis, and C. Jusitaniae, although C. albicans tends to be the most commonly implicated organism in mucocutaneous infections. C. albicans is a dimorphic fungus that causes a variety of infections in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients, including mucocutaneous infections and invasive blood stream infections, or urinary tract infections. It can phenotypically switch from yeast to hyphae based upon the temperature. T lymphocytes play an important role in preventing fungal infections, so a deficiency of T lymphocytes predisposes to fungal infection. Fungal elements are recognized by antigen presenting cells (APC) through interaction with C-lectin receptors. Interactions between APCs and CDB+ T lymphocytes activate these cells for direct cytotoxic killing; they also induce them to release interleukin-17 (IL-17), which promotes T helper 17 (Thu) cell proliferation. These cells produce IL-17 and IL-22, which attract neutrophils, which are also fungicidal. Additional cytokines released during this also induce development of Th 1 cells, which have been shown to play a role in fungal immunity.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Decreased B-lymphocyte activity (Choice A) is seen in disorders such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia and results in deficient humeral immunity. These patients are at higher risk for invasive bacterial infections. Decreased dendritic cell activity (Choice B) would predispose to infection with bacteria, viruses, and fungi. Dendritic cells are APCs that interact with T and B lymphocytes to present antigens necessary for both cellular and humeral immunity. Alternatively, increased dendritic cell activity (Choice F) would result in activation of both B and T lymphocytes and would not cause an immunodeficiency syndrome, although overactivation may be associated with autoimmune disorders. Decreased segmented neutrophil function (Choice C) is seen in a variety of disorders and may include defects in neutrophil chemotaxis or function. Patients present with recurrent bacterial infections. Increased segmented neutrophil function (Choice G) would not cause an immunodeficiency syndrome. Increased B-lymphocyte activity (Choice E) is seen in response to bacterial and viral infection as these cells differentiate into memory B lymphocytes and plasma cells to secrete immunoglobulins, which are important for attenuating future infections. Increased T-lymphocyte activity (Choice H) is associated with some autoimmune conditions but does not lead to an increased risk for fungal infections. Educational Objective: T lymphocytes play an important role in the control of fungal organisms. Cytotoxic CDB+ T lymphocytes, Th 1 cells, and Th 17 cells all play a role, thus deficiency in T-lymphocyte function increases the risk for both mucocutaneous and invasive fungal infections.

questionStem: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his parents are concerned that he has had several episodes of tripping and incoordination over the past 10 months . He has high-arched feet and hammer toes . His father also has high-arched feet and a history of distal extremity weakness . His mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus and severe diabetic neuropathy. Examination of the patient shows mild weakness of the hand musculature and weakness and wasting of the anterior tibial and intrinsic foot muscles . Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the ankles and decreased elsewhere . Sensation to vibration and proprioception are mildly decreased over the distal lower extremities . Motor nerve conduction velocities are markedly decreased with prolonged distal motor latencies in the extremities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's weakness?
correctExplanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) is a heritable disease of peripheral neuropathy. As a result of primarily autosomal dominant mutations in genes expressed in Schwann cells, the myelinating cells of the peripheral nervous system, peripheral sensory and motor nerves become progressively demyelinated. Patients demonstrate motor weakness and decreased sensation to vibration and proprioception most prominent in the distal lower extremities. Physical examination findings include hyporeflexia or areflexia, along with clumsy walking and consequent musculoskeletal deformities such as pes cavus (high arch of the foot) and hammer toes (toes with an abnormal upward bend of the middle joint). Later in the disease course, atrophy of the lower extremity muscles and intrinsic hand muscle weakness and atrophy may occur. Diagnosis occurs via nerve conduction studies, which may show decreased conduction velocities and prolonged distal motor latencies consistent with demyelinating disease (some disease subtypes show decreased amplitudes suggestive of axonal loss). Treatment is supportive and includes physical therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Choice B) is an acquired, immune-mediated disease of the peripheral nerve roots that leads to symmetric proximal and distal motor weakness and decreased sensation to vibration and proprioception. The course may be relapsing-remitting or progressive. In this patient with a family history suggestive of peripheral neuropathy, CMT is more likely. Diabetic neuropathy (Choice C) is an acquired, symmetric polyneuropathy that predominantly affects the sensory nerves of the distal lower and upper extremities. Motor weakness typically occurs only in severe cases, after years of hyperglycemia. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Choice D), caused by an inherited mutation in the dystrophin gene, typically presents at age 2 to 3 years with progressive muscle weakness affecting the proximal more than the distal muscles. Cardiac conduction abnormalities are also common. Sensory neuropathy would be atypical. Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (Choice E) an inherited muscular dystrophy resulting in slowly progressive, asymmetric muscle weakness in the facial, scapular, upper arm, lower leg, and abdominal muscles. Sensory neuropathy would be atypical. Educational Objective: In Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, an autosomal dominant mutation expressed in Schwann cells leads to symmetric motor and sensory polyneuropathy that begins in the distal lower extremities and may progress to the upper extremities. Muscle weakness typically results in hyporeflexia and progresses to muscle atrophy. Sensation to vibration and proprioception is frequently affected. Patients demonstrate a clumsy gait and consequent skeletal deformities such as pes cavus and hammer toes.
